II.            BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
 
Comments of the Committee
 
            The Committee notes the Department’s contention that funds could not be utilized under Adult Education mainly because of failure of North-Eastern States to use the funds, particularly under continuing Education
Programme.  The Committee has been informed that the bulk of the allocation was made under Continuing Education Programme and except Tripura, none of the other states in North-Eastern region could progress to the
Continuing Education Programme stage and hence, nearly entire allocation for NER during 2004-05 and 2005-06 remained unutilized.
 It is a matter of great concern that none of the NE states, other than Tripura, could progress to the Continuing Education Programme stage.  The Committee is of the considered opinion that such a dismal performance by
the NE States is in fact a poor reflection on performance as well as planning.  Moreover, it seems that the Department was not vigilant enough about such a position in North-Eastern Region, otherwise, they would not have been
caught unawares in this regard.  Department ought to have been more careful. The Committee recommends that the Department do the needful to prevent recurrence of such disturbing development.                           
                                                                        (Para 2.5)
 
Comments of the Committee
 
Apprehension of the Committee about increase in the number of pending utilization certificates in 2005-06 when compared with the pendency position in 2004-05 have proved to be true with regard to the Adult Education
Programme.  The Committee views with serious concern the massive increase in the amount of pending UCs from Rs. 140.12 crore in 2004-05 to Rs. 704.50 crore at the end of 2005-06.  The Committee would emphasize once
again the need for urgent steps to be taken for elimination of pending UCs.                                                   (Para 2.6)
 
III.            SARVA SHIKSHA ABHIYAN
 
Comments of the Committee
 
            The Committee notes that expenditure reported by the States/UTs under SSA for 2005-06 has been Rs. 9993.35 crore, which is 77 percent of available funds.  The Committee feels that this by no means can be treated as a
decent achievement in face of the fact that SSA, a flagship scheme of the Department, had already overshot the time schedule.  Such a pace certainly does not augur well for the success of the Abhiyan.  After an analysis, the
Committee also notes that there are only 13 States/UTs out of all the 35 States/UTs which have been able to utilize 80 or more percent of the available funds.  This situation, the Committee feels, call for the Department to be
more pro-active, vigilant and sincere to ensure optimum utilization of funds as well as achievement of physical targets under various components of the SSA.
            The Committee has been given to understand that financial progress of the programme is reviewed and expenditure levels are closely monitored every quarter by the Department SSA funds are to be transmitted from State
level to villages/schools/blocks and cluster centres.  The Committee would, however, like to point out that these compulsions cannot justify the ever increasing amount of unspent balances. The very fact that unspent balances are
there indicates that financial targets are not being achieved.  The Committee is, therefore, of the opinion that the Department should make every effort for optimum and judicious utilization of allocated funds.                        
                                                            (Para 3.6 & 3.7)
 
Comments of the Committee
 
            The Committee appreciates the efforts of the Department to cater to educational needs of children with special needs (CWSN) under the SSA. However, the Committee feels that more and more such fully equipped
schools for such children need to be opened under SSA.  The Committee recommends that more and more teachers be made to undergo longer duration training on Inclusive Education.  It strongly feels that there is an urgent need
to create a database regardingnumber/percentage of CWSN in variousschools so that teachers specially trained for this purpose could be posted adequately in such schools.                (Para 3.16)
 
Comments of the Committee
 
The Committee is of the considered opinion that apart from universalizing elementary education, the SSA must lay added emphasis on quality of teaching- learning also.  Only then the SSA will be really successful.  The
lack of trained teachers is also a major factor resulting in dismal quality of education.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the efforts for having child-centred padagogy and competency based teaching must be given
added impetus.  In addition to this, in- service training should be provided to the teachers more frequently.
(Para 3.21)

CHAPTER - I
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY GOVERNMENT
II.            BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
Recommendations/Observations
2.6            Committee’s attention has been drawn by a disturbing trend gradually taking roots along with the increase in
allocation and utilisation of funds.  The Committee observes that as on 1.4.2004, there were as many as 4652 pending
Utilisation Certificates for an amount of Rs.5510.85 crore.  While appreciating the persistent efforts made by the
Department in getting reduced the pending UCs to 2903 amounting to Rs.535.62 crore, the very fact that there are pending
UCs highlights the inadequacies of the accounting procedure as well as incapacity of the implementing agencies.  Another
comparatively more serious fall-out being noticed is increasing unspent balances lying with various Grantee institutions. 
The Committee is constrained to observe that there were unspent balances of Rs. 505.53 crore as on 1.4.2005 which
reached the figure of Rs. 928.86 crore within a short span of 6 months.  The Committee cannot but conclude that this
figure must have increased further by the closing of 20.5.06.  What is more worrisome is that major portion of these
unspent balance is from Plan funds that too with other implementing agencies (NGOs)/autonomous bodies.  The
Committee is of the firm view that along with the projection for enhanced funds, the Department needs to take every
precaution not to allow such a tendency of unspent balances which is against all the financial norms.
Action Taken
            As far as the receipt of Utilization Certificates are concerned, additional checks have been introduced at the pre-
payment stage in the light of MoF. O.M. No.7(3)/E.Coord/2006 dated 8.8.2006, to ensure that no grant is released to a
grantee against whom Utilization Certificate is pending. A Utilization Certificate Monitoring System has been placed
(giving details of pending Utilization Certificates) on the internet to facilitate checks at sanction stage.
            Unspent balances lying with State Governments and other implementing agencies are invariably taken into account
while making further releases.  In this connection, it may be mentioned that during the period from 1.4.2005 to 30.9.2005,
the grants released were of the order of Rs.2584.08 crore (Plan - Rs.1063.22 crore and Non-Plan - Rs.1520.86 crore).
During the same period the various implementing agencies had utilized an amount of Rs.2160.75 crore, thus leaving an
unspent balance of Rs.928.86 crore.  The level of unspent balance came down to Rs.697.82 crore (Rs.282.78 crore with
State Governments and Rs.415.04 crore with other implementing agencies) as on 31.03.2006.  It may be mentioned that an
amount of Rs.342.74 crore was available only after the 3rd and final batch of supplementries and funds could be
transferred only in the last week of March, 2006.  It may also be mentioned that funds lying with other implementing
agencies are mostly with various autonomous bodies like IITs, NITs, IISc, NVS, KVS etc.  However, every effort is made
to ensure that unspent balances are kept to the minimum.
IV.            NATIONAL COUNCIL OF EDUCATIONAL RESEARCH AND TRAINING (NCERT)
Recommendations/Observations
4.5       The Committee recommends that NCERT should take all possible steps to plug the loopholes in the distribution of
textbooks, as they are already aware of the weak areas in the distribution of textbooks and ensure that students get
textbooks on time.

Action Taken
            The present position of distribution and proposed steps to ensure easy availability of NCERT textbooks from the
coming academic session 2006-2007 are as follows:
(i)         There are 235 distribution outlets of wholesale agents all over the country for             NCERT publications,
catering to 7904 schools.
(ii)        A large number of non-recognized schools are also using NCERT textbooks.              These books are also used by
candidates appearing for various competitive             examinations.  Therefore, a cushion is proposed to be maintained by
adding 20%             more than the requirement by CBSE affiliated schools. 
(iii)       States using NCERT textbooks are advised to take the copyright from NCERT to         print the number of books
themselves as per their requirement.
(iv)            NCERT textbooks are proposed to be sent to far flung areas first so that they can             be released
simultaneously from all the outlets.
(v)            Textbooks are proposed to be printed in adequate quantity by February, 07 to             ensure that they are
available before the start of the academic session 2007-08 in    April, 07.
(vi)            Instructions will be issued to all distribution outlets to collect their requirement of             NCERT textbooks
from the month of January, 07 instead of waiting for the             seasonal demand in March/April.
XV.            NATIONAL COUNCIL OF RURAL INSTITUTES
Recommendations/Observations
15.4     The Committee has strong reservations on the way the Council is being run.   The Committee strongly feels that
final view needs to be taken and basic requirements for the effective functioning of the Council need to be fulfilled without
any further delay.
Action Taken
            The observation of the Committee has been noted. The Council is fully functional even though for technical
reasons and pending finalization of Recruitment Rules in consultation with the Ministry of Law, the Recruitment Rules are
yet to be notified. The Council has approved 09 projects proposal during the year 2005-06 including setting up of Center
of Excellence in Gandhian Studies in three Vidyapeeths at Pune, Banaras and Ahmedabad. Therefore, the Ministry would
reassure the Committee that in keeping with Committee’s desire and suggestions to see that the institute starts functioning
effectively on a regular basis, the Council has also been reconstituted with eminent persons.
XVI.    ALL INDIA COUNCIL FOR TECHNICAL EDUCATION (AICTE)
Recommendations/Observations
16.3     The Committee is given to understand that for management courses the institutions/universities are under the dual
control of UGC and AICTE.  Many a times, this dual control creates problems for smooth conduct of the management
courses.  The Committee feels that the Department should come up with a framework to ensure that there is no conflict in
the working of any statutory bodies.
Action Taken
            The Council through the Act of Parliament is vested with the powers and functions to:
-
         lay down norms and standards for courses, curricula, physical and infrastructural facilities, staff pattern, staff
qualifications, quality instructions, assessment and examination [section 10 (i)];
 
-
         Grant approval for starting new Technical Institutions and for introduction of new courses or programmes in
consultation with the Agencies concerned [section 10 (k)];
 
-
         Inspect, cause to inspect any Technical Institutions [section 10 (p)];
 
-
         for the purposes of ascertaining the financial needs of technical institution or a University or its standards of
teaching, examination and research, the Council may cause an inspection of any Department or Departments of
such Technical Institution or University to be made in such  manner as may be prescribed and by such person or
persons as it may direct [11(1)].
 
            However as per Hon’ble Supreme Court Judgment in Bharathidasan University and Another v/s AICTE and others
“AICTE Act 1987 section 10 (1) (k), 2(h), (i) & 23 Act does not required a university to obtain prior approval of AICTE
for starting a department or unit as an adjunct to the university itself to conduct technical education courses of its choice-
Regulations framed under Act requiring the University to obtain such approval, held, void and unenforceable- However,
University obliged to conform to the standards and norms laid down by AICTE-All India Council for Technical Education
(Grant of Approval for Starting New Technical Institutions, Introduction of Courses or Programmes and Approval of
Intake Capacity of Seats for the Courses or Programmes)”. Therefore it has been observed that some Universities are

188th report of human resource development
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/188threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:32:36]
starting Technical Education Programmes without the involvement of the Council.  The Universities come under the
control of UGC.
            The norms of the Council in respect of universities including deemed to be universities as per its notification dated
November 28, 2005 state “No University including Deemed University shall conduct technical courses/programmes
without ensuring maintenance of the norms and standards prescribed by AICTE”.
            The MHRD has also issued notification no. F. 2-1/2006 U.3 (A) dated April 7, 2006 clarifying this issue
(Annexure-V).
XVIII.    INDIAN INSTITUTE OF MANAGEMENT (IIMs)
Recommendations/Observations
18.5     The Committee was informed that currently, IIMs at Ahmedabed, Bangalore and Kolkata are generating their own
resources for their functioning.  Government provides financial assistance both under plan and non-plan to IIMs at Indore,
Lucknow and Kozhikode.  The Committee recommends that the government should chalk out a plan in consultation with
IIMs to ensure that over a period of time the IIMs become                 self-supporting and not depend on government for
normal functioning. 
Action Taken
            As a measure to provide greater autonomy in the functioning of the Centrally funded Higher Educational
Institutions of importance, the Ministry, with the approval of the Competent Authority, has decided to introduce, inter-
alia, in IIMs, a Scheme of Block Grant (Non-Plan) for a period of five years from 2005-06. These IIMs shall be allowed to
retain the Internal Revenue / Income generated by them and their entitlement for annual grant-in-aid during the Block
Grant period shall not be adjusted against any increase in income. The Government would provide matching grant
equivalent to the annual savings from the regular non-plan grant and other receipts including internal revenue and earnings
from consultancy, entrance examination like CAT etc. and other continuing education programmes but, excluding receipts
earmarked for designated purposes in accordance with the terms & conditions of such donations with due approval of the
Finance Committee & Board of Governors. The matching grant would be available till the Endowment Fund has reached
the level of Rs.50.00 crore in respect of each of the IIMs. Matching grant equivalent to the total savings transferred to the
Endowment Fund in a Financial Year shall be sanctioned to the Institute in the following Financial Year.

20.1     Under this scheme, scholarships are awarded to students from non-Hindi speaking States/UTs for pursuing post-
matric studies in Hindi. The Committee notes that 2426 scholarships involving an expenditure of Rs.89,63,519 were
awarded to students of different States during 2005-06. The Committee has been given to understand that under this
scheme the States are reporting only total expenditure incurred by them each year.  The Committee is not aware whether
any exercise has been undertaken so far for making an assessment about the implementation of this scheme as per the
prescribed norms. The Committee would also like to point that as per the records available for 2005-06, only 7 renewal
scholarships were awarded. This clearly shows that students are not showing an inclination for pursuing the study in Hindi

            For making the scheme more effective and popular, the Scheme of Scholarships to Students from Non-Hindi

sanction of fresh as well as the renewal scholarships in respect of those scholarships holders, who had been sanctioned
scholarships in the earlier years and funds were released to the States/UTs in terms of proposal received from them for

them to ensure that scholarships once granted to the students in the initial year of a particular stage of education are
invariably renewed during the subsequent years, within the same stage of education.

XVII.            SCHEME OF COMMUNITY POLYTECHNICS
Recommendations/Observations
17.5     The Committee notes that more than 300 polytechnics are having unspent balances lying with them. Therefore, the
budget allocation was reduced at the RE stage in 2005-06. Non-utilization of the allocations to that extent indicates that the
scheme is plagued with constraints/drawbacks. The Committee recommends that if need be, the scheme may be revamped
to ensure that the entire allocations are utilized by the polytechnics. A serious review of the scheme of things would help
in finding the utility of the scheme for the targeted beneficiaries and also the aspect of fund utilization. 
17.6     The Committee is also disappointed to note that the Community Polytechnics are not evenly distributed across the
country. The situation is particularly poor in the Eastern Region which has the maximum rural populace but this region has
been accorded with only 97 Community Polytechnics of the total 669 existing in the country. The Committee would like
the Department to ensure that there is an even regional distribution of the Community Polytechnics so that technology
becomes the real carrier of community/rural development.  
Action Taken
            The Ministry has initiated action to review the Scheme. A meeting was held with all State Government
representatives in December, 2005 to explore various options for continuing the scheme beyond the 10th Plan, including
restructuring the scheme, or transferring this Scheme to the State Sector at the end of the 10th Plan. It was decided in the
meeting to constitute a Working Group under AICTE to review the Scheme. The working group has submitted its
recommendations and the matter is being considered in the Ministry.
            The Scheme of Community Polytechnics is implemented only through AICTE approved Diploma Level
Institutions (Polytechnics) which are under the Administrative Control of State Governments. As there are less number of
approved polytechnic level institutions in the Eastern Region compared to other regions, the number of Community
Polytechnics are also less. Further, since AICTE has delegated the powers to open new Polytechnics to the State
Governments, the action for opening new Polytechnics will have to be taken by the State Governments. As per the
information received from the State Directorates of Technical Education, most of the Govt./Govt. Aided Polytechnics of
the States of Eastern Region have been covered under the Scheme. As and when new Polytechnics are opened in the
Eastern Region, the Ministry can consider including these under the Scheme of Community Polytechnics, after
restructuring the Scheme.
            The issue of expanding the Scheme's coverage in the Eastern Region was also raised by the Department related
Parliamentary Standing Committee on HRD previously, in it's 145th Report. Pursuant to the Committee's observation, the
Department had engaged in an exercise to consult the concerned State Governments as well as AICTE on this issue and a
meeting was also organised by AICTE with representatives of State Directorates of Technical Education of the concerned
States. The State Government representatives observed that increasing the number of Polytechnics in the Region may not
be possible. However all of them were of the view that more extension centers may be allowed in the region under existing
Community Polytechnics to cover a larger area. This option will be considered at the time of restructuring the Scheme.

Recommendations/Observations
19.2     Under the scheme out of the proposed 10976 total scholarships, 9012 scholarships for class IX and 13830 out of
proposed 17000 scholarships of class XII were granted during 2005-06, incurring an expenditure of Rs.7,50,61,198.  The
Committee appreciates that this scheme has finally taken off, specially in view of its non-performance under the two
erstwhile schemes till 2004-05.  The Committee observes that almost all the States/UTs have been covered under this

renewal scholarships granted in 2005-06 is only 788, out of which as many as 713 going to Haryana.  The Committee
would like to emphasize that the very objective of the scheme would be lost if the meritorious students getting scholarship
in class IX or XI do not get the benefit in the next class.  The Committee is not aware about the past experience in this
regard.   The Committee would, however, like to emphasise that this aspect needs to be given due consideration.   The

Action Taken
            Since the National Merit Scholarship Scheme, which was effective from 01.04.2004, was notified only by
16.02.2005, i.e. at the fag end of the financial year 2004-05, the proposals for release of funds under the National Merit
Scholarship Scheme could be processed only with effect from the financial year 2005-06.  Hence, the renewal scholarships
in respect of this scheme will mainly materialize during the current financial year 2006-07. As regards non-renewal of
scholarships granted under erstwhile National Scholarship Scheme (NSS) and Scheme of Scholarships at Secondary Stage
for Talented Children from Rural Areas, it is stated that renewal of scholarships is sanctioned on the basis of specific
proposals received from the States/UTs in this regard. Here, it may also be added that the guidelines of the National Merit
Scholarship Scheme (NMSS) and of its predecessor schemes, viz. National Scholarship Scheme (NSS) and Scheme of
Scholarships at Secondary Stage for Talented Children for Rural Areas were circulated to the States/UTs every year,
regularly. In such circulars, the State/UTs were requested to furnish proposal for sanction of fresh as well as the renewal
scholarships in respect of those scholarships holders, who had been sanctioned scholarships in the earlier years and funds
were released to the States/UTs in terms of proposal received from them for fresh scholarships as well as for renewal
scholarships. The National Merit Scholarship Scheme is implemented through States/UTs. As per the guidelines of the
Scheme, the continuance/renewal of scholarship under the scheme is performance dependent and depends on the
promotion of the awardee to the next class, provide he/she secures 60% or more marks in aggregate in Science/Commerce
Stream and 55% or more marks in aggregate in the Arts/Humanities Stream in Semester/Annual Examination, which
determines his/her promotion to the next class. Further, good conduct and regular in attendance is a pre-requisite for
continuance of the scholarship. The decision of the State Government/UT Administration in this regard, is final and
binding in all such matters. The pace of renewal has been slow on account of the fact that the State/UTs concerned have
not furnished adequate proposals for renewal of scholarships for reasons best know to them. 
            The National Merit Scholarship Scheme and the Grant-in-aid Scheme of Scholarships to Students from Non-Hindi
Speaking States/UTs for Post Matric Studies in Hindi have been placed on the Ministry’s Website
www.education.nic.in/scho.htm

            UNIVERSITY GRANTS COMMISSION
Recommendations/Observations
12.4     The Committee was informed that out of the total UGC expenditure amounting to Rs. 1943.56 crore for the year
2004-05, an amount of Rs. 460.04 crore was disbursed to the state universities and colleges which constitute 23.67% of the
total expenditure.  The Committee notes that the financial position of the state universities is poor so much so that a major
chunk of allocated funds goes to salary and allowances and maintenance expenditures.  There is little left for these
universities to undertake research and quality improvement of education.  Unfortunately, University Grants Commission is
not maintaining any data regarding the fund allocation by the State Governments to the State Universities which prevents
in getting a clear picture of the financial position of the State Universities. The Committee recommends that the UGC
should maintain a database of the funding pattern of the state universities. 
Action Taken
            Resource Crunch in State Universities is a matter of concern. The University Grants Commission provides
development assistance to the State Universities under Section 12.B of the UGC Act, 1956.  At present, there are 217 State
Universities, out of which 119 Universities are being given development grant. The outlay for 2006-07 to the UGC has
been considerably increased to enable higher assistance by the Commission to universities by way of development grants.
            The development (Plan) grant by UGC to the State Universities is for supplementing general infrastructure viz.
buildings, purchase of equipments, books and journals and, to some extent, for teaching faculty for the given plan period. 
The UGC does not make any grants for salaries or maintenance to State Universities as these institutions are to be
maintained by the respective State Government. 
            It is true that the University Grants Commission was not maintaining any data hitherto regarding the fund
allocation by the State Governments to the State Universities.  The recommendation of the Committee has been noted. 
The University Grants Commission has written to all the State Universities to furnish information regarding the fund
allocated by the State Government to them and the major items on which the said amount is spent.  The Universities will
also be requested by the Commission to include such information in their XI Plan proposals.  The information would
thereafter form the database on the funding pattern of State Universities.
Comments of the Committee
            The Committee appreciates the efforts to collect information about funds allocated to and the expenditure of the
State universities.  But the Committee notes that hardly Rs. 3 - 4 crore were given to 119 State Universities out of about
Rs. 460 crore in 2004-05 as Development Grant. Whatever fund is given by the State Governments are used up in paying
salaries, pensions and other non-plan expenses. The purposes for which UGC gives money are all highly capital-intensive. 
This situation, the Committee, feels needs to be considered by the Centre, States and the UGC for coming out with
comprehensive proposals.

supply situation, quality, connectivity with infrastructure distance from the main cities etc. Different State Governments
evolve different mechanism to fill the vacant seats.

students do not come forward to get admission in such colleges due to poor faculty, infrastructure, distance, etc.  The
Committee does not expect that the Government to force the parents/students to go to these colleges/institutions.  It
certainly expects the Government to force the AICTE to ensure that no colleges having substandard infrastructure/faculty,
etc. are approved and these are asked to improve their quality.  The Committee feels that it is not a situation of supply
exceeding the demand, it is infact otherwise today.
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
16.7     As per the Expenditure Budget of the Department for 2005-06, an amount of Rs.91.48 crore has been allocated
under the Plan head for reorganising, restructuring and strengthening AICTE, Bureau of Technical Education and its

Committee and Boards.  On a query, the Department informed that there was no such proposal. Thereafter the Committee
sought further clarification in this regard from the Department. In response, the Department has clarified that “the
functions of the AICTE is to ensure coordinated and integrated development of technical and management education and
maintenance of standards. Government supports the activities of AICTE through budgetary supports. Grants are released
on lump sum basis to AICTE and AICTE in turn allocates fund under various schemes”.
 
16.8     The Committee is not satisfied with the comments of the Department. The reply of the Department does not clarify
why the fund was allotted to a non-existent programme. It is amply clear that a provision of Rs.91.48 crore was made in
the budget without any purpose. This, according to the Committee is a clear case of financial/budgetary irregularity. An
enquiry may be made into the entire episode and the findings may be furnished to the Committee. 
 
Action Taken
 
               The Department related Parliamentary Standing Committee has observed that the reply of the Ministry that the 
Government supports the activities of the AICTE through budgetary support and grants are released to the Council for 
funding their various schemes does not clarify as to why the funds were allotted to the non-existent programme.
 
               In this regard it is stated that the AICTE was established by an Act of the Parliament i.e. the All India Council for 
Technical Education Act, 1987. The powers and functions of the Council include ensuring coordinated and integrated 
development of technical and management education and maintenance of standards etc. Section 16(1) provides that the 
Council shall have its own Fund and also sums which may from time to time be paid to it by the Central Government, shall 
be credited to the Fund and all payments by the Council shall be made therefrom. The AICTE has its own mechanism of 
approval of schemes i.e., approval of Executive Council etc. Section 10(c) provides that the Council may allocate and 
disburse out of the fund of the Council such grants on such terms and conditions as it may think fit to:
 
(i)               Technical Institutions, and 
 
(ii)               Universities imparting technical education in coordination with the                Commission. 
 
               The Funds to the AICTE are allocated under Plan schemes on lump sum basis after internal discussion on the 
proposals in this Ministry and the Planning Commission. Then the AICTE allocates the Funds Schemes-wise. It is not that 
a sum of Rs.91.48 crore was released to AICTE for the first time. During 2004-05, a sum of Rs.54 crore was released to 
the AICTE.  Not only at the BE stage, the progress of expenditure of the Council is reviewed even at the RE stage also. 
During 2004-05 there was an unspent balance of Rs.6 crore, therefore, the budgeted provision of Rs.60 crore was reduced 
to Rs.54 crore. The Government, during the last four years, has released funds on lump-sum basis to the AICTE as under:
 
Year Rs. in crore
2002-03 90

2004-05 54
2005-06 91.48
With regard to specific release of fund during the year 2005-06, it is stated that the AICTE had forwarded Plan proposals 
for a sum of Rs.136.14 crore for taking up various schemes during that year. As against that, a sum of Rs.91.48 crore was 
provided for AICTE  schemes as Plan funds. 
 
               AICTE incurred an expenditure of Rs.96.80 crore by way of releases to various Technical 
Institutions/Universities/Organizations under various approved funding schemes, as per its power under Section 10 (c) of 
the AICTE Act.  Similarly during the earlier year i.e. 2004-05, AICTE had incurred an expenditure of Rs.54.63 crore 
against the release of funds of Rs.54 crore. The details of funds allotted by the AICTE to different Schemes during 2004-
05 and 2005-06 are enclosed at Annexure VI.
 
               It is therefore, not correct to say that Rs.91.48 crore sanctioned by MHRD during the financial year 2005-06 to 
AICTE as Plan fund was without any purpose.

Recommendations/Observations
16.1     The Government of India constituted a Central Committee under the Chairpersonship of the Secretary, Ministry of

Harassment of Women at Workplace. The Committee in its Meeting held on 29.10.2002 recommended that Awareness needs

Welfare Board alongwith Ministry of Information and Broadcasting. The National Commission for Women has taken up

3.22     The Committee would like the Ministry to take cognizance of the observations contained in the Mid Term Appraisal
and take immediate remedial measures to streamline the scheme. The Committee desires that it may be apprised about the

Action Taken
 
A few actionable points which emerged out of the Mid Term Appraisal of the Scheme were as under:-        
(i)
                 Restructuring of ICDS
(ii)                Strengthening of pre-school education under ICDS
(iii)              Integration of ANM and Anganwadi worker
 
i.  Restructuring of ICDS: The ICDS Scheme envisages Anganwadi Workers to be honorary workers from local community
who are paid fixed amount of monthly honoraria for rendering their services, on part time basis (for about 4-5 hours in a day)
whereas Creche functions throughout the day on regular basis. Adding Crèche and Day care services/facilities in Anganwadi
would require full day/regular Anganwadi Workers who might claim regular salary or minimum wages. At present there are
more than 14 lakh AWWs and Helpers. This number would increase to over 19 lakh with the proposed expansion of the ICDS
Scheme. On the other hand, there are only a few thousand crèches across the country at present. As such, provision of crèche
and day care service/facilities in Anganwadis does not appear feasible as of now. However, this suggestion would be
examined further and, if found feasible, would be included in our proposal for continuation of ICDS Scheme in the XI Plan.
 
ii. Strengthening pre-school Education under ICDS: The training component under ICDS has been strengthened. The training
syllabus for Anganwadi Workers has also been suitably revised to serve the need of pre-school education component of ICDS.
Deptt. of Elementary Education has issued instructions to all State Secretaries to organize joint training of Primary teachers,
AWWs and health workers for a convergent understanding of pre-school and ECCE. The suggestion to involve the State
Councils for Educational Research and Training (SCERTs) in training of Anganwadi Workers is very good and necessary
action would be taken accordingly.
 
iii. Integration of ANM and Anganwadi Worker: The ICDS Scheme envisages Anganwadi Workers to be honorary workers
from local community who are paid fixed amount of monthly honoraria for rendering their services, on part time basis (for
about 4-5 hours in a day). There is no minimum qualification prescribed for Anganwadi Worker. While the exact data on
educational qualification of Anganwadi Workers in position is not available, as per informal feedback, there is a significant
number of Anganwadi workers who are semi-literate.  The appraisal note does not also indicate the State-wise number of
ANMs sanctioned and in position so as to see the ratio between the two.  It may be noted that under National Rural Health
Mission (NRHM), a health volunteer viz. ASHA is being appointed at the village level.  Bringing AWW under the ANM will
not only drive away the former from her original role and responsibilities under the ICDS Scheme but will also dilute the
delivery of other important services under the scheme viz. supplementary nutrition and pre-school education. The Ministry of
Women and Child Development, therefore,  does not support the integration of the ANM and AWW.
 
Comments of the Committee
 
The Committee does not quite agree with the contention of the Ministry about (i) providing day care/creche facilities at
Anganwadi Centres and (ii) about coordination of Anganwadi Workers and Auxiliary Nurse Midwives(ANM)/ASHA. The
Committee reiterates its recommendation to further examine these suggestions for implementation.

Relief and Rehabilitation of Victims of Rape
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
15.5     The Committee feels that the victims of rape undergo the conditions of psychological stress and trauma
notwithstanding the physical assault. The rehabilitation process of such victim involves psychological support as well as
economic assistance. The Committee would like the Ministry to create a separate rehabilitation fund for victims of rape to
ensure that they get all sort of psychological and economic assistance in time.
 
Action Taken
 
As per the draft scheme under the consideration of this Ministry for providing relief and rehabilitation to the victims of rape,
Criminal Injuries Relief and Rehabilitation Board is proposed to be constituted district-wise in all States under the
chairpersonship of the District Magistrate or District Collector to consider claims from rape victims and award relief,
including interim compensation. It is also proposed to constitute District Monitoring Committees to arrange medical and legal
aid to the victim, her shelter, protection and rehabilitation. These Committees will have counselors, medical doctors and
lawyers to assist the victim. One of the functions of the Committee will be to arrange for psychological and medical aid and
counseling to the victim. The Criminal Injuries Relief and Rehabilitation Board constituted at the district level, upon receipt of
the application and after having been prima facie satisfied that a case of rape has been made out and making a preliminary
assessment about the nature of the claim, shall order, as far possible, within a period of three weeks from the date of receipt of
application, an interim financial relief of Rs.20,000/-. The amount of final relief will be awarded by the Board taking into
consideration the needs of the victim, the expenses incurred or likely to be incurred in connection with medical treatment,
psychological counseling, abortion, if it is resorted to in consequence of rape, loss suffered on account of cessation or
interruption of employment or gainful activity, expenses on provision of alternate accommodation, if any and compensation
for damage, pain, trauma, humiliation or inconvenience. The ceiling of the final amount of relief is proposed to be fixed Rs.
2.00 lakhs. However, a provision is included in the draft scheme to raise the maximum amount of final compensation to
Rs.3.00 lakhs in exceptional cases by the National Criminal Injuries Relief and Rehabilitation Board constituted at the Central
level. Though no creation of a separate fund is proposed in the scheme, the proposal to release adequate amount as interim
compensation to the victim within a reasonable time frame and the amount of final compensation upto Rs.3.00 lakhs proposed
to be paid to the victim would help mitigate her sufferings.
Comments of the Committee
 
The Committee is not satisfied with the reply of the Ministry.  The Committee reiterates that separate rehabilitation fund for
Victims of Rape should be created from the next financial year.

1.1 The Department of Health incurs expenditure, either directly or through various
institutions and establishments run by it, and also by way of grants given to autonomous and
voluntary organisations. Grants to States and Union Territory administrations are mainly for
Centrally Sponsored Health Schemes being implemented through State Governments and
Union territory administrations. These include national programmes for prevention, coutrol
and eradication of diseases, particularly the communicable ones.

1.2 Centrally Sponsored Health Schemes, financed 100% by the Central Government,
are the National Schemes for Prevention of Visual Impairment and Blindness, including
Trachoma, National Leprosy Eradication Programme, National Guinea/worm Eradication
programme and National AIDS Control Programme, etc.

1.3 Schemes on which the expenditure is shared between the Central Governmest and
the State Governments on 50 : 50 basis are the National Malaria Eradication Programme
(Rural and Urban), Sexually Transmitted Diseases Control Programme, National
T.B. Control Programme and Kala Azar Control Programme.

1.4 Besides running some hospitals and dispensaries, the Department finances, wholly
or substantially, some autonomous Institutions engaged in patient care and/or medical
research, such as AIIMS, ICMR, JIPMER, Pondicherry, AIIPMER, Bombay, PGIMER,
Chandigarh, Central Councils for Research in Ayurveda and Siddha, Unani, Joga and
Naturopathy and Homeopathy, etc.

1.5 It has set up National Institutes separately for various systems of Indian Medicine
and Homeopathy. Two Public Sector Undertakings (i) Indian Medicine Pharmaceutical
Corporation Ltd.; and (ii) Hospital Services Consultancy Corporation (India) Ltd., have also
been set up by the Department. Voluntary Organisations and Institutions, substantially
assisted by the Department, are the Indian Red Cross Society, New Delhi, Tuberculosis
Centres, New Delhi, Lala Ramsarup Tuberculosis Hospital, Mehrauli, etc.

1.6 The Secretariat of the Department of Health, mainly engaged in policy formulation,
is advised on the broad policy matters by the Central Councial of Health, set up under
Article 263 of the Constitution. The Health Ministers of Stastes are its members. Technical
expertise on medical and public health matters is provided by the Directorate General of
Health Services, an attached office of the Ministry. The Directorate General of Health
Services is also responsible for implementation of programmes through its subordinate
offices, including Hospitals, Medical Stores Depots, Drugs Controiler, Training and
Research Institutions, etc.

2. The Committee notes that the total outlay of the Department for the year 1995-96 is
Rs. 1048.16 crores of which Rs. 644.57 crores is under plan and Rs. 403.59 under non-plan.

The Committee was informed that the allocation for the Department of health constituted
0.06% of the total budget of the Government of India for 1995-96.


2.1 When asked about the reasor for providing less in the non-plan this year, it was
explained by the Department that the non-Plan budget for 1994-95, which was increased to
Rs. 408.09 crores in the RE, included provision of Rs. 24.00 crores to accommodate the grant
from Germany for Rajiv Gandhi Institute of Cancer Research, New Delhi. This, being
national and cae-time grant, was not a part of the regular budget. In other words, the actual
non-Plan budget of the Department was Rs. 384.89 crores which has been enhanced to
Rs. 403.59 crores in 1995-96 i.e. an increase of 4.86% over the previous year’s budget
provision.

2.2 Similarly, regarding allocation, on the revenue side, the Secretary, Department of
Health, explained that it also included Rs. 75 crores of German aid which was to be received
in terms of equipment in the year 1995-96. So, for the purpose of comparison, he argued,
Rs. 75 crores had to be deducted from the RE of the last year.

2.3 The Committee is deeply concerned over such a meagre allocation (i.e. 0.06% of the
total budget) for Health, which forms an important ingredient of human development. The
WHO has recommended that the public health care expenditure should be at least 5% of the
GDP, if equity and universal coverage has to be realised. Public expenditure in health sector
in India, both by the Centre and the States, however, has been a litte over 1.5% of the GDP.
The Committee hopes that the Government would make efforts to achieve the target of
spending 5% of the GDP on Health sector by the year 2000 AD.

2.4 The Committee feels that the allocation for the Department of health, though shows
an increase this year over the previous year, does not appear to be adequate in view of India’s
commitment to attain ‘Health for All’ by 2000 A.D. With the present rate of increase, the
Committee apprehends, that ‘Health of All’ would remain a distant goal. The Committee,
therefore, feels that if at all the Government is serious about this, it should try to find out
ways and means for providing a suitable share to the Health sector from the GDP every year.

2.5 The Committee observed that, generally, non-plan expenditure has been going up
leaps and bounds resulting, sometimes, in diversion of plan funds to the non-plan expenditure,
which is not a healthy practice. When asked about this, the Department stated that there had
been a rising trend in the prices of medicines and other consumables, which being non-plan
expenditure, had an edge on demands for higher allocation. In view of this factor, the Ministry
of finance was requested to make necessary additional allocations at the R.E. stage. the
Department, however, had not made any diversion of funds from plan to non-plan to meet the
increased expenditure under non-plan. The Committee is happy to note that no such diversion
of funds was resorted to by the Department.

Medical Education and Training

3. The Committee wanted to know if the total outlay provided for Medical Education,
Training and Research in the year 1995-96, was less than what was provided last year. It was
explained to the Committee that it was not, if compared to the BE of the last year. While an
outlay of Rs. 258.26 crores was provided in BE 1994-95, Rs. 277.77 crores has been provided
for this purpose in BE 1995-96. As regards increasing the allocation to Rs. 322.84 crores at RE
level, the Committee was informed that this allocation also included the component of
German aid which was one-time grant.

3.1 The Committee notes that the allocation for Medical Education Research and Training
included outlays mainly for premier institutions like AIIMS, PGIMER, Chandigarh, MCI and
ICMR, etc, which are the back-bone of medical research and training in our country. In view of
the shortage of trained medical and para-medical specialis! manpower in the country and the
urgent need for strengthening the base of medical research, the allocation for this purpose, the
Committee feels, is not adequate and it should, therciore, be suitably increased.


3.2 In the context of growing number of private medical Colleges, the Committee
recommends creation of proper monitoring machinery to supervise their function. It also
emphasises the need for strengthening the MCI.

Cancer Research

4. There is reduction in allocation for Cancer research from
Rs. 19.80 lakhs in the BE, 1994-95 to Rs. 16.88 crores in BE 1995-96. When questioned; the
Secretary, Department of Health, stated that the allocation had to be reduced as the
Department was not giving now any recurring grants but was only giving a lump-sum of
Rs. 50 lakhs per year to various hospitals and regional cancer centres for establishing Cobalt
units and opening of Oncology wings in various medical colleges.

4.1 The Commitiee is not satisfied with the answer given by the Secretary regarding the
cut in the allocation for Cancer research. Cancer treatment, in fact, requires highly
sophisticated and costly equipment which is not available even in reputed Government
Hospitals. In view of the cancer treatment becoming expensive, there is an imperative need
to provide adequate facilities for this. The Committee, therefore, recommends an increase in
allocation for this purpose from the next year and regional cancer centres given more funds.

63 In vespouse to the Committee’s suggestion in para 57 of its Report, given last year,

serious exception.

National Institute of Ayurveda, Jaipur

nen-plan) was provided in the BE 1994-95. The Committee notes that allocation for the

deputed immediately to take stock of the situation and review the progress of the Institute
end prepare a report so that steps may be initiated to clear the augean stables at the earliest.
The Committee also recommends that a suitable enhancement be made in the allocation for
this Institute at the RE stage.


7.4 The Committee is happy to learn, that on the initiative of the Department, the pay-
scales of teachers have recently been upgraded and hopes that the posts lying vacant in

National Institute of Siddha

Institute of Siddha has been received from the State Government of Tamil Nadu. The

that the proposal of Tamil Nadu Government be examined expeditiously and funds provided

Mental Health

9. The institutions/hospitals working in the field of Mental Health are in a pathetic
condition. These are not being given adequate financial and other support. Even the meagre
amount given for mental health was not being utilised properly. The Committee notes that
the allocation for this purpose has remained more or less stagnant for the last two years.

9.1 The Committee, in its 9th Report submitted in 1994-95, had expressed its concern
over the poor state of affairs in the field of mental health care and had recommended (para
35) to ensure a minimum standard of treatment to the mental patients.

9.2 During the course of evidence, the Secretary, Department of Health, informed the
Committee that the National Mental Health Programme, initiated during the 7th Five Year
Plan, aimed at making available mental health care services, by identifying some medical
colleges for imparting training in basic knowledge in this field, to the primary health care
physicians and para-medical personnel. Besides, adequate attention is also being given to
premier institutions like the CIP, Ranchi, National Institute of Mental Health & Nurro
Sciences, Bangalore and the Institute of Human Behaviour and Allied Sciences, Sahadara,
Delhi. The NIMHNS, Bangalore, has been provided Rs. 10 lakhs for conducting training
programmes for physicians engaged in mental health care.

9.3 The Committee was also informed that some mental hospitals were visited by the
Secretary, Department of Health, and the DGHS, on the directions of the Supreme Court,
and after visiting these hospitals, a scheme has been submitted which envisages, among other
Measures, some autonomy to these hospitals. Other recommendations are under implemen-
tation.

9.4 The Committee expresses its concern over the unsatisfactory conditions prevailing in
the institutes/hospitals meant for mental health care and research. The training programme
evolved by the Centre has also not picked up. The response from the State Governments is
neither forthcoming nor adequate. 5

9.5 The Committee feels that the need for improving the services and facilities for
treatment and training and extending them upto the district and primary health care level
can hardly be ignored. There is an imperative need for having a comprehensive plan for
tackling the mental health problems in this country. The Committee, therefore, recommends
that a programme be evolved with broad thrust on improving the status of mental health
care services in our country, by involving mental hospitals, departments of psychiatry in
medical colleges, training of medical and para-medical staff and creating awareness among
the people.

Central Institute of Psychiatry, Ranchi

10. The outlay provided for the CIP, Ranchi, has been much less than what was
demanded during 1994-95 and also in 1995-96. Against a demand of Rs. 2.94 crores under


plan this year, only 1.50 crores has been provided. It is also less than Rs. 1.60 crores
provided in the RE last year.

10.1 As regards the gap between the amount projected and the amount provided, the
Department contended that the demand, particularly under the non-plan, was on the higher
side and was not supported by the trend of expenditure during the previous years.

10.2 The Committee is not convinced by the argument advanced by the Department for
giving much less than what Was asked for by the Institute. It feels that the Department
should have ensured that the funds provided to the institute were utilized properly. The
Committee is aware of the poor conditions obtaining in the Institute and, in fact, last year
also, in its Ninth Report, it had drawn the attention of the Department to this issue and had
recommended that a review of the functioning of the Institute be conducted soon.

10.3 When asked about the action taken in this regard, the Committee was informed
that in pursuance of its recommendation, a work study of the Institute had been proposed
and the Ministry of Finance had been requested to nominate a core member from the Staff

10.4 The Committee recommends that the Department should review the financial
requirements of the Institute at the appropriate stage and enhance the outlay based on its
actual needs. It also likes the Department to ensure that the Institute does utilise the fund
fully and properly. The Committee also recommends that the formalities regarding
constituting the proposed study group should be completed early and the work be started.
The study group should be asked, the Committee suggests, to make concrete and positive
suggestions for bringing about radical improvements in the functioning of the Institute.
Yoga

10.5 The Committee is of the view that the Department has not made desired efforts to
provide facilities for Yoga therapy/training for treatment of various diseases and mainte-
nance of health in our country. There is a greater need to provide yogic treatment in
diseases like Diabetes, Asthama, Arthritis, hypertension, etc., in the present context. The
Committee, therefore, recommends that the new Department of ISM&H should take
concerted steps in this regard. Popularisation of Yoga Therapy, Committee feels, needs
immediate attention.

Hospitals & Dispensaries

11. The Committee notes that the total allocation of Rs. 79.93 crores in 1995-96 for
Hospitals and Dispensaries in allopathy though Higher in comparison to the amount of Rs.
75.59 crores provided in the BE 1994-95, is less than Rs. 92.14 crores provided in the RE of
the same year. When asked, the Secretary Department of Health, explained to the
Committee that this decrease was more apparent than real because the RE of 1994-95 also
included an element of aid given by Germany to purchase equipments, which was a one time
grant. In actual practice, therefore, there is no decrease in outlay in 1995-96.

11.1 The Committee is fully aware of the appalling conditions prevailing in the Central
Government Hospitals. Facilities and services being provided are both inadequate and sub-
standard. Modern and sophisticated equipments are either not there or are not working.
Problems like lack of staff and basic amenities to the patients are known to everyone. About
the dispensaries, the less said the better.

11.2 The Committee is of the opinion that mismanagement of both men and materials is
the major cause for all the ills bedevilling our hospitals and dispensaries. With this level of


allocation to the hospitals and dispensaries, the Committee feels, it would not be possible to
maintain even the existing services, what to think of expanding of improving them. It,
therefore, recommends that a realistic assessment of the requirement of all the hospitals and
dispensaries be madc and a suitable amount be provided at the RE level.

11.3 There is much to be desired in the functioning of the prestigeous medical
institutions under Central Government control, like AIIMS, Safdarjung Hospital, Lady
Hardinge Hospital and PGIMER frequent strikes and work stoppages, both by doctors,
para-medical staff and others are the order of the day. Indifferent management and
indiscipline aggravate the problem. This is highly deplarable. But, the committee is not
going deep at this stage, into the functioning of the Central Government Hospitals and
dispensaries as well as the Central Government Health Scheme, as a special study of the
same has been undertaken by the Committee and the report thereon is under preparation.

Vallabbhai Patel Chest Institute

12. It is a premier institution devoted to applied and basic research and referral clinic
for chest diseases. The Committee notices a decline in the fund earmarked for this Institute,
as compared to that in the RE of 1994-95,

12.1 The Committee was informed that the functioning of the Institute was reviewed on
two occasions in 1994 and it was decided to enhance the non-plan budget by Rs. 60.00 lakhs
for the year 1994-95 and also to provide a sum of Rs. 27.00 lakhs under plan for revival of
its activities and also for modernising its labs, etc.

12.2 In view of the rising level of air pollution and resultant high incidence of
respiratory and related diseases, the Committee feels that even the increased amount
provided for the institute will not be sufficient to carry out its obligations.

12.3 Several complaints regarding lack of drugs, misuse of funds, maladministration, etc.
in the Institute were brought to the notice of the Department by the Committee. The
Secretary, Department of Health, assured the Committee that he would look into them but
he denied any misuse of funds having come to his notice during the reviews done by him last
year. He said: “The fact is that there is no money to pay electricity bill, to pay telephone
bills... to pay salaries because the non-plan funds were not increased and the plan funds
were totally zero. This Institute is virtually starved of funds.....This Institute certainly needs
more money.”

12.4 In view of the above admission by the Secretary, the Committee is distressed to
conclude that a premier Institute, which had done a lot of outstanding scientific work in the
areas of chest diseases like TB and Asthma and which had large number of international
publications to its credit, is being allowed to languish in this manner.

12.5 The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that the Department should
prepare, after a careful study, a comprehensive plan to develop and modernise the Institute’s
laboratories with a view to reviving the research activities and restoring its previous glory.
The Department should assess the financial requirements for impiementing that plan and
make suitable provision in the Institute’s Budget at the appropriate stage.

National Health Program
National Malaria Eradication Programme

15. This programme is a centrally sponsored scheme on 50:50 sharing basis with the
States. The Committee notes with roncern that the malaria situation in the country had not


improved even after the adoption of Modified Plan of Operation (MPO) strategy from 1977.
The Committee observed from the following statistics supplied by the Department

Year Malaria cases (Million) Deaths
1976 6.47 59
1984 2.18 247
1987 1.66 188
1989 2.05 268
1990 2.02 353
1991 कं 421
1992 213 422
1993 2.20 345
1994 2.20 1069

that except in the years 1991 and 1992, the total number of cases of malaria had gone up
over the previous years. Similarly, deaths due to malaria had also increased consistently,
except in the years 1984 and 1992.

15.1 The Committee does not agree with the Department’s contention that containing
malaria cases to around 2 million per year, from 1984 onwards, was in itself an indication of
the success of the programme. The aim of the programme, the Committee points out, is not
merely containment but its eradication. Even the containment theory does not hold good, as
the incidence of malaria has increased all these years. The Committee is not satisfied with
the explanation given for the outbreak of malaria in Rajasthan last year, which led to an
unsurge in deaths due to malaria in 1994.

15.2 Insecticidal spray is the main component of the strategy adopted under NMEP, but
not many States were achieving the target fixed in this regard. Reasons attributed for this
are: refusal to spray by the community; delay in release of funds by the States leading to
delay in procurement of insecticides; lack of funds to meet operational works; and large
number of vacancies of malaria staff.

15.3 The Secretary, Department of Health, during his evidence before the Committee,
stated that the main constraint in implementing NMEP successfully was lack of adequate
response and cooperation from the States. While the Centre was giving a lot of support,
technical and logistic, including insecticides, drugs, equipment, etc., to the States, actual
implementation rested with the States only.

15.4 The Committee is of the opinion that the outlay for NMEP, though increased in
1995-96, is not adequate only Rs. 119 crores on the plan side has been given against a
demand of Rs. 182 crores for this purpose. Even the Secretary, Department of Health, also
accepted that the amount provided was not sufficient and the programme, in fact, needed
more.

15.5 The Committee, therefore, recommends that more funds should be provided for
this programme. It also emphasises the need for activating the administrative machinery
from the top to bottom and recommends that all out efforts be made for tackling the menace
of malaria on‘the level it was done during the 60s.

15.6 When enquired about the progress regarding the project for 100% assistance from

World bank for control of malaria in the tribal areas of seven States, Andhra Pradesh,
Gujrat, M.P., Bihar, Rajasthan, Maharashtra and Orissa, the Committee was informed that


necessary information as required by World Bank are being collected for finalising the
proposal. The Committee finds that this proposal is pending for a long time. The
Committee, therefore, suggests that the Department should collect the required information
and get the proposal finalised without any further delay.

15.7 The Committee advises the Department to take the help of elected Panchayats and
local volunteers, and involve teachers, particularly in tribal and remote areas, for making
NMEP a success. All the PHC, the Committee recommends, be provided trained manpower
for preparing slides, microscopes, enough drugs and insecticides. If malaria can almost be
eradicated during the 60s. when the country did not have enough infrastructure, it can be
done with much ease today.

National Leprosy Eradication Programme

16. This programme is a 100% Centrally Sponsored Scheme and is implemented with an
aim to achieve elimination of leprosy by the year 2000 AD; thereby reducing the leprosy
caseload in the community to 1/0000 population.

16.1 Rs. 80 crores has been earmarked for this programme in 1995-96 (BE), as against
Rs, 94 crores provided in the RE of 1994-95. The Committee was informed that the
programme was provided Rs. 14 crores in 1985-86 and since :then allocations to the
programme had increased gradually to Rs. 35 crores in 1993-94. The government secured
IDA assistance of Rs. 302 crores for six years for expansion of the programme in 1994.
Accordingly, the programme budget was steeply hiked to Rs. 94 crores in 1994-95. With this
fund, adequate infrastructural support, drugs, vehicles and other logistics have been
provided to all the districts throughout the country during 1994-95. Thus, the programme
would not require any expansion or increased expenditure on logistics during 1995-96, hence,
the decrease in its outlay. Rs 80 crores provided this year is only for consolidation and
sustaining the on-going anti-leprosy activities.

16.2 The Committee expresses its satisfaction over the performance of the natioanal
Leprosy Eradication Programme and is happy to learn that the registered leprosy caseload
had come down from 11.6 lakh cases at the end of March, 1994 to less than 8 lakh cases
now. The Committee also notes that with the application of Multi-drug Therapy (MDT),
which makes the patient non-infective very soon, has reduced the duration of the whole
treatment. There is more voluntary reporting now and the cases are being reported at early
stages.

16.3 The Committee emphasises the need for maintaining the pace of success in this
regard and advises the Department to guard against the feeling of contentment as was
noticed in the case of NMEP. The Committee recommends that adequate emphasis: be
provided to the rehabilitative aspect also in which voluntary organisations should be involved
in a big way.

17.1 The Committee is happy that blood bank services are being improved. The

Committee emphasises the urgent need of improving blood transfusion services and making
them foolproof so that no HIV-infected blood was given to anyone as more and more such

cases are being reported now-a-days. Disposable needles, it has ‘been observed, are not being
used in all the hospitals/dispensaries. The Committee recommends that the use of such
disposable Syringes should be enncouraged and adequate emphasis be given on surveillance
and clinical management. Increased stress should be given for voluntary blood donation.

Plague Control

18. Outbreak of plague last year, after remaining dormant for several decades, had taken
everyone by surprise. When asked as to what contingency and long term plan the Department
had for preventing recurrance of this dreaded disease, the Department stated that a technical
Advisory Committee to determine factors for the outbreak of Plague and to avoid its
recurrence in future had been constituted in 1994, which is expected to submit its final report
by April 1995.

18.1 As a follow-up action, government has initiated activities like surveillance, training
of workers and upgradation of laboratories. Surat Medical College, Surat, B.J. Medical
College, Pune, Grant Medical College, Bombay, S.R.T.R. Medical College, Beed, and
Bangalore Medical College, Bangalore, have been provided financial assistance for develop-
ment of laboratory ficilities. In addition, National Institute of Communicable Diseases, Delhi,
has also been strengthened by providing financial assistance for the development of their
laboratory facilities.

18.2 The Committee notes that the Medical Colleges selected for the development of lab
facilities fall in the endemic area in which Plague cases were reported first. Possibility of it
occurring in other parts of the country cannot be ruled out. The Committee, therefore,
suggests that such assitance be provided to all regional laboratories in different parts of the
country so that cases could be detected promptly and remedial and preventive measures taken
without wastage of time.

National T.B. Control Programme

19. Under the programme, a fully equipped and staffed District T.B. Centre is being set
up in each district of the country. The Committee was informed that such T.B. Centres have
been set up in 85% districts of the country so far. A proposal is under consideration of
expansion of District - B programme to the remaining districts in a phased manner by 2000
AD. Infrastructure under TB programme, as on December 1992 and December 1994, are as
under:—

Centres Clinics Beds
December, 92 386 331 47321
December, 94 390 327 47409

19.1 When enquired about the slow pace of progress in regard to setting up of DTCs, TB
Clinics, etc., the Department explained that for the last three years emphasis was on
consolidating infrastructural facilities and capabilities created already for the implementation
of the programme.

19.2 In response to a query regarding allocation for this programme, the Secretary,
Department of Health, stated that the allocation for TB control had been increased in 1995-96
and a littler more money was made available last year also. He claimed that “something
fantastic” could be done in TB control if more funds were made available to the Department.


19.3 The Committee found the progress in regard to increasing the DTCs, TB clinics
etc. very slow. It also notes that though the programme is being implemented since 1962.
So far only 85% districts-of the country could be covered and the rest are expected to be
covered by 2000 AD. Mortality rate due to T.B., which has come down from 80 per lakh
of population in 1968 to 50 per lakh of population, now,-is also not very satisfactory.

19.4 Despite all these efforts and achievements, the Committee observes, with deep
concern, that the incidence of T.B. does not appear to have come down drastically; it
remains, more or less, constant. T.B. is not more a killer disease and it can be cured
completely if a proper regimen of medicines and life style are adhered to.

19.5 The Committee recommends that the matter of setting up DTCs in the remaining
districts should be taken up with the respective State Governments and more and more
T.B. clinics should be provided in the rural areas. The Committee also suggests that for
the detection of T.B., the Department should rely more on microscopy method that on
radiology because quite often diagnoses, based on the latter technique, were found to be
wrong, particularly in the case of pulmonary T.B.

19.6 The Committee also recommends increase in the allocation for the National T.B.
control Programme through preventive measures from early childhood.

De-addiction Centres

20. The Committee noticed that the outlay for De-addiction Centres have been
reduced by Rs. 50 lakhs in the BE of 1995-96, than what was provided the last year. The
Department explained that this reduction had to be effected because the Department got
much less than what it had projected.

20.1 When asked about the recommendations of the Committee made last year to
open more De-addiction centres, the Committee was informed that this programme was
reviewed by the Expenditure Finance Committee in October, 1994 which endorsed the
Ministry’s view to continue the assistance under the Central sector to State Governments
for establishment/strengthening of Drug De-addiction Centres in Medical Colleges/district
level hospitals and that extra measures be taken to stengthen the infrastructure in NE
States. During 1994-95, 8 new centres were proposed to be set up two of which will be in
NE region.

20.2 The Committee feels that neither the number of De-addiction centres nor the
infrastructure provided to them in adequate. It also feels that the outlay for this purpose
should not have been reduced.

20.3 The Committee reiterates its recommendation to open more sub-centres in
various parts of the country. The efforts shoule be to provide one such centre in every
district having the facilities for detoxification and psychological counselling. The Committee
feels that the number of beds for this purpose is also inadequate and it should be
increased. The Committee, therefore, recommends suitable increase in the outlay for the
Drug De-addiction centres at the RE level.

National Iodine Deficiency Programme

21. The National Iodine Deficiency Disorders Control Programme is a purely Central
Scheme which envisages availability of iodised salt in place of common salt for human
consumption to all segments of the population. The target fixed for achieving universal
iodisation of salt, the Committee was informed, could not be met within the stipulated
period which was 31st December, 1992. The reasons given for this was that some States/


UTs had not yet issued/enforced the notifications banning the sale of non-iodised salt. The
Committee was assured that as soon as all the States/UTs enforce the’ ban, the production of
iodised salt would be stepped up according to the demand and the scheme of iodisation
would be simultaneously extended to cover all the regions of the country.

21.1 The Committee finds the implementation of the universalisation of iodised salt
tardy. The Committee is not aware as to why some of the States were not taking intrest in
the programme. It recommends that the Department should intervene in a more positive and
effective manner for persuading the States to implement the scheme in the current year. A
sustained publicity campaign should be conducted to create awareness among the peaple.

CHAPTER - I
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY GOVERNMENT
 
II. BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
Recommendations/Observations
 
2.4    The Committee can afford to conclude that even the formulation of a quarterly annual action plan for 2005-2006 by the
Ministry has not been able to achieve the desired results. It’s the case of failure in planning. It appears to the Committee that the
Ministry remained engaged in projecting higher requirements and launching new schemes without any considerations of the
judicious and optimum utilization of funds allocated for the existing schemes. It is quite contradictory that on one hand the
Ministry talk of resource crunch and on other hand the allocated resources are not fully utilized. Huge unspent balances are lying
with the Ministry under various schemes. This fiscal disorder in the Ministry has done more harm. The case for higher allocations
has weakened to a great extent. The Committee is of the view that a detailed review of all the ongoing schemes should be
undertaken so as to assess the shortcomings being noticed and take remedial steps for removal of the same. Active involvement of
the State Governments and other implementing agencies in this exercise is called for. The Committee would like the Ministry to
adopt better fiscal management practices to avoid the last minute spending for achieving the targets.
 
Action Taken
 
The advice of the Committee is accepted.
 
V. NATIONAL SERVICE SCHEME
 
Recommendations/Observations
      
5.6       The role of State Liaison Cells is conceived as the fountainhead for ensuring timely release of grants, monitoring and
liaison with the universities and +2 level councils. Non-existence of such Liaison Cells in some States itself indicates the plight of
NSS activities. Perhaps the Ministry has failed to persuade the States/Uts in setting up such an important functionary of the
scheme. The Committee would like the Ministry to impress upon the States the importance of the Liaisoning Cells and take up the
matter at the highest level of those States not having set up these cells so far.
 
5.7       The Committee finds that this scheme is also plagued with the problem of unspent balances. A total of Rs.4.99 crore of
unspent balance is pending with various States such as Assam, Bihar, Jharkhand, Delhi, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh and
Punjab. Major defaulter being Bihar, Jharkhand and Punjab which account for more than 3.60 crore as shown below:-

XIV.
        SCHEME FOR DOPE TEST
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
14.1     The scheme aims at prevention of drug abuse in sports by providing technical facility for Dope Test. Under the scheme, it
has been decided to set up two independent autonomous agencies namely National Anti-Doping Agency (NADA) and National
Dope Control Laboratory (NDCL) and provision has, accordingly, been made keeping in view their technical and administrative
requirements. SAI has developed the Sports Science Centre at Patiala, Bangalore, Calcutta, Delhi and Gandhinagar. These Centres
mostly provide scientific support to the national campers, SAI Training Centre inmates and are also involved in research and
teaching.
 
14.2 The Committee was informed that there was some delay in procurement of equipments for Dope tests since the scheme was
under revision. The financial allocation under the scheme was also reduced due to postponement of accreditation process by
WADA and consequent less purchase of equipments. An allocation of Rs.5.00 crore has been made for 2006-07 against an
allocation of BE Rs.10.20 crore and RE Rs. 3.70 crore during 2005-06.    
 
14.3
          The Committee is constrained to note that at present, SAI has only 38 Sports Scientists including medical doctors. This
strength of scientific personnel is not enough to provide optimum scientific support to the sports needs in the country. Sports-
related scientific research and development in India has not been able to keep pace with international developments in various
fields like Physiology, Psychology, Bio-mechanics etc. Greater attention is required to be given to research and development of
sports science, in case India has to excel in sports at international level.  
 
14.4
          The Committee is happy to note that in view of the Commonwealth Games, 2010 the anti-doping programme has been put
on fast track. A number of important steps to check the increasing incidences of doping are proposed to be taken by the
Government which include:-
 
(i)
          According high priority to education of athletes;
