5.5       SCHEME OF COMMUNITY POLYTECHNICS
Recommendations/observations
5.5.1    The Scheme of Community Polytechnics was started during the year 1978-79 as a direct Central Assistances Scheme of the
Government of India (Ministry of Human Resource Development) with the aim of harnessing the scientific/technical knowledge
available with Polytechnics to secure Community /Rural Development.
5.5.2    The Committee is happy to note that the a Working Group constituted to review the scheme of Community polytechnics has
since given its recommendation and the Department is in the process of considering them while restructuring the scheme for
implementation in the 11
th Plan. As per the information made available to the Committee, some of the major recommendations of
the Working Group include upward revision of financial norms of the scheme including remuneration to project staff of the
scheme; strengthening the infrastructure at regional monitoring agencies of the scheme ie., NITTTRs; appointment of exclusive
officers at the State Directorate of Technical Education for monitoring the scheme; improvement of data flow and documentation
on the achievement of the scheme to enable wider adoption of best practices; emphasis on promotion of rural entrepreneurship and
development of micro enterprises and development of competency based curricula for effective skill transfer. The Committee
however did not find any mention of any recommendation to address the problem of uneven distribution of Community
Polytechnics in the country. Of the 669 Community Polytechnics in the country, the Eastern region has the least number i.e., 97 of
them compared to the North, West and South which have 187, 145 and 240 respectively. This position was even more disturbing
for the fact that the Eastern region was a backward region having the highest concentration of rural population. To a specific query
in this regard, the Department accepted the fact that all the Govt./Govt.-aided polytechnics of the North-Eastern region have not
been covered under the scheme. Out of a total number of 29 such polytechnics in the region, as many as 10 of them were yet to be
covered under the scheme. The Department has informed that these polytechnics could not be covered under the scheme since there
was no provision for expansion in the approved scheme during the 10
th Plan period. The Committee recalls that the Department on
the insistence of the Committee had taken up the matter of augmenting the strength of Community Polytechnics in the North-
Eastern region with the concerned State Governments. The Department in its action taken report to the Committee had then stated
that the State Governments had expressed their inability to open fresh Polytechnics but could consider opening more extension
counters of the existing polytechnics in that region. 
5.5.3    The Committee is of the considered opinion that the uneven reach of the Scheme in the Eastern region of the country does
not conform to its objective of securing community/rural development. The Committee, therefore, urges the Department to factor
in this aspect while reviewing the Scheme for the 11th Plan.
Action Taken
            The Recommendation of the Committee has been noted and will be considered while reviewing and revamping the scheme
during the XIth Five Year Plan.

respective research projects.
3.3.2    The Committee has come across a number of irregularities in the functioning of the Institute.  The Department in a Special

fellowships are determined by the 'Governing Body' according to the directives of the Government issued from time to time and in
the light of revision of emoluments of fellows in other research organization of the M/o Human Resource Development. Unlike the
Indian Council for Historical Research (ICHR) which contains a stipulation in its Research Funding Rules that a candidate who is
selected for fellowship would require to furnish an undertaking in a prescribed proforma to the effect that if he leaves the
fellowship prematurely in the midway without completing the research project/manuscripts, he would have to refund the entire
amount of fellowship paid to him till that date.   This condition binds the fellow to complete the research work/monographs.  In the

3.3.3    Another disturbing fact brought out in the Special Audit Report is that as many as 37 fellows had not submitted their
monographs or their monographs were not worth publication or the fellows got the monographs published on their own.  Thus the

expenditure to the tune of Rs.93.36 lakh on fellowship grants paid to fellows.

and blockage of funds to the extent of Rs.200 lakh due to slow progress of special repair and maintenance of R.P. Niwas.

3.5       FAKE UNIVERSITIES
Recommendations/observations
3.5.1    According to the UGC Act, 1956, the right of conferring or granting degrees shall be exercised only by a University
established or incorporated by or under a Central Act, or a State Act, or an Institution deemed to be University or an institution
specially empowered by an Act of Parliament to confer or grant degrees. Similarly, no institution other than a University
established or incorporated by or under a Central Act, or a State Act shall be entitled to have the word ‘University’ associated with
its name in any matter whatsoever.
3.5.2    To a specific query regarding the fake Universities identified and the action taken against them, the Department in its reply
stated that the UGC has detected 19 fake Universities/Institutions which are operating in violation of Section 22 of the UGC Act,

CHAPTER - III
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/202ndreport.htm[01-07-2016 15:44:46]
1956. The Department has further informed that out of these 19 fake Universities/Institutions, the UGC is yet to initiate legal
proceedings in respect of 6 of them, namely Gandhi Hindi Vidyapith, Allahabad (U.P.); DDB Sanskrit University, Puttur(T.N.); St.
John’s University, Kishanattam (Kerala); Raja Arabic University, Nagpur; Keserwani Vidyapith, Jabalpur and ADR-Centric
Judicial University, New Delhi, for want of full relevant details about these institutions.
3.5.3    A perusal of the status of the legal proceedings initiated against the 13 fake Universities/Institutions reveals that in most of
the cases, proceedings are likely to continue for long. In some cases, UGC is awaiting replies from the State Governments whereas
in some other cases, response is awaited from the police authorities. In the other cases, sessions of stays-counter stays, affidavits-
counter affidavits are on between the UGC and the fake Universities/Institutions. 
3.5.4    The Committee is of the considered opinion that the delay in the settlement of the cases gives rise to a situation of utter
confusion wherein both the parties claim to be on the right side of the law.  As a result, fake Universities/Institutions are taking
advantage of this confusion and continue to cheat the public. The Committee, therefore, urges the Department to take expeditious
action against fake universities/institutions under the existing regulations and rules.  Necessary legal sanctions be put in place
including by approaching Parliament for this purpose.  The Committee also strongly feels that there is an urgent need for giving
wide publicity about the existence of such fake universities.  Merely putting the list of approved universities on the website of UGC
will not serve the purpose.  Both Department and UGC need to be more pro-active in this regard simply because future of our
young students is involved.
Action Taken (paras 3.5.1 to 3.5.4)
In view of the observations of the Hon'ble Committee, the matter since been taken up with the University Grants Commission
(UGC) again requesting them to be more proactive in getting the fake universities/institutions closed down as early as possible.  
Since such institutions operate in violation of the UGC Act, 1956, it is incumbent on the part of the UGC to tackle such illegal
activities and, if necessary, to lodge FIR with the police as soon as the existence of such institutions comes to its notice.   This
Ministry has again directed UGC on 9
th August, 2007 to take a more proactive role in getting the fake universities/institutions
closed down as early as possible as there was inordinate delay in initiating legal action in as many as 6 cases and the proceedings in
13 other cases were also found to be conducted in a lackadaisical manner.  The UGC has also been advised to strengthen its
Malpractices Cell and to make it more accountable.  The need for starting more vigorous campaign in the print media against fake
universities/institutions has also been emphasized.
            The UGC has informed that it has issued Public Notice/Press Release in June, 2007 through some leading Newspapers,
cautioning the aspiring students about the fake Universities identified by it.
            The Ministry of Human Resources Development is separately formulating a proposal for strengthening the existing legal
framework with a view to ensuring deterrent punishment to fake institutions that function in contravention of the UGC Act, 1956.
Comments of the Committee
(paras 3.5.1 to 3.5.4)
The Committee notes that the Department has put the blame squarely upon the UGC for not being able to deal with the
problem in an efficient and effective manner. It, however, feels that the UGC is perhaps unable to take appropriate action in this
regard due to lack of adequate and stringent legal measures which the Department has indicated to be working on.  The Committee,
therefore, calls upon the Department to expedite the process for strengthening of the existing legal framework to pin down such
fake universities.  The Committee would also appreciate if a status note on the progress made in the legal proceedings initiated/to
be initiated against the 19 fake universities identified by UGC, is submitted to it at the earliest.  The Committee would like to point
out that there is an urgent need for making student/parents aware about existence of such fake universities.   A mechanism can
easily be evolved by seeking the co-operation of State Education Departments.

            The Committee is dismayed to note that the 10 th Plan proposals of IGNOU were approved as late as October, 2004 when
half of the Plan period was over. The Committee finds such a delay ridiculous. It would like the Department to give details of the
quarterly monitoring mechanism it intends to set up so as to assess the physical and financial targets of IGNOU.
Recommendations/observations
4.1.6    The Committee notes that at present, 10 Central  Universities, 20 Deemed Universities, 87 State  Universities (including
State Open Universities) and 2 Institutes of National Importance are offering education through distance mode. On a specific query
about the existence of any monitoring mechanism for evaluation of various courses of distance education, the Committee was
informed that all such institutions have been notified from time to time to get their programmes approved by the Distance
Education Council. The Committee is surprised to note that inspite of there being a three tier process for recognition of institutions
and approval of their programmes, course materials from 90 institutions have been received so far and only about 300 programmes
have been approved so far. The Committee would like to impress upon the Distance Education Council to take immediate steps for
approval of all the remaining courses yet to be approved. The Committee would also like to be apprised about the number of
institutions offering courses yet to be approved by DEC and action, if any, taken so far. The Committee is also of the opinion that
there is a need for making student community aware about the existence of unapproved institutions of distance education.  This is
all the more required in the emerging scenario when increasing number of students would be opting for Distance Education
courses.
Action Taken
Distance Education Council (DEC) is in the process of revising its guidelines for recognition of distance education institutes and
the distance education programmes.   The Council, in light of the revised guidelines, shall take necessary action.   DEC has also
initiated discussion involving experts for accreditation of the distance learning institutions in order to ensure quality.   It has been
informed by DEC that 101 institutions/universities have applied for recognition.  Out of these institutions, 34 were recognised, 23
were rejected and the cases of remaining 44 institutions are pending.
            Department fully agrees with the concern of the Committee that there is need to make student community aware about the
existence of the unapproved distance education institutions.  DEC, in this regard has refereed to an interim injunction of Hon'ble
Himachal Pradesh High Court, inter-alia stating that IGNOU, which it-self a university can not monitor the other universities
offering distance education programmes.  To rectify this, it is proposed to grant independent statutory status to DEC.
Comments of the Committee
The Committee views with serious concern the unduly long process of granting of recognition to Institutions/Universities
offering education through distance mode.  Out of 101 applications for recognition, only 34 institutions have been recognised, 23
have been rejected and the cases of remaining 44 institutions are pending.  The Committee would like to impress upon the Council
to expedite this recognition process.  The Committee would also appreciate if a status note on the follow-up action taken against
the de-recognised Institutions/Universities is furnished to it at the earliest.   The Committee would also like the Department to
provide detailed information regarding the total number of distance education institutions that are functioning in the Central, State
and private domains.   
Department's fully agreeing with the concern of the Committee about the need for making student community aware about
the existence of unapproved distance education institutions would not serve the purpose.  Need of the hour is pro-active approach
on the part of all concerned.
The Committee would like to remind the Department that it had, in its 172
nd Report on 'University and Higher Education',
stressed on the need for giving the DEC an independent statutory status like the UGC. Till date, the Department has been assuring
the Committee regarding action in this regard but nothing appears to have happened. The Committee, therefore, urges the
Department to take expeditious action in the matter.

Recommendations/observations
 
5.3.3    A major problem area noticed in technical education was that the seats in a number of institutions remained unfilled every
year due to non-availability of eligible students. To a query as to what mechanism was being contemplated by the Department to
solve the problem of seats remaining unfilled in technical institutions, the Department informed that the Central Government did
not interfere in the admission process of the centrally funded technical institutions. Admissions to AICTE approved institutes were
within the purview of State Governments.  State Governments evolve their own policy for filling up of the vacant seats.  Admission
to IITs is done through Joint Entrance Exams and all decisions regarding admission are taken by the Joint Admission Boards.

Central Counseling Board frames the policy for admission in these Institutes. 
5.3.4    The Committee finds the reply of the Department not convincing.   Holding the States responsible for the seats which
remain unfilled, tells only one side of the story. The Department must appreciate the fact that the tendency of allowing seats to go
unfilled is sheer wastage of scarce national resources. The need to curb this tendency becomes even more necessary given the
sectoral imbalances in terms of availability of opportunities and the uneven density of professional educational institutions in some
of the States. The Committee, therefore, recommends that suitable mechanism may be worked out in consultation with the States. 
The institution which generally default in filling the entire quota of the seats may be warned and their intake capacity may be
reduced to the extent of unfilled seats.  The concerned bodies must be asked to evolve suitable mechanism to ensure that seats do
not remain vacant in our technical institutions.

states.

Department in the matter.   The Committee, however, at the least expects the Department to ensure that the AICTE works out an
effective strategy in a time bound manner.

Recommendations/observations
 
7.1       The Committee notes with concern that no allocation what so ever have been made for the National Programme for Women
during the year 2007-08. The Department in response to this query has informed the Committee that the Scheme was formulated
during the 10
th Plan. There were various components of the Scheme like the provision for Hostel, right from schooling stage to
University stage; scholarships; and Study Centres besides others. When the Scheme was reviewed by the Department, it was felt
that these Schemes were already in existence under various programmes. For instance, in school education, there was a scheme for
assistance to NGOs for girls hostels. The UGC also had a scheme for hostels. Therefore, the decision was taken that each of these
components be strengthened under the existing schemes.  The UGC runs a part-time associateship to women Ph.D holders who do
not get employment or cannot have full time job.
 
7.2       The Committee does not accept the reply of the Department. While the Department has been prudent enough to realize
duplication of its efforts in improving access of women to higher education, it has failed to redesign the programme to improve
women education and allocate funds in the Demands for Grants. The Committee is of the view that a more cautious approach
should have been taken in this regard especially when the matter pertains to making provisions for women. The Committee,
therefore, recommends that a proper strategy and programme may be chalked out to benefit the women in higher education.
7.3       The Committee further notes that a Standing Committee has been constituted to undertake a review of the prevailing status
of the Women’s studies centres in the country and to assess the role the Centre have played in consistence with the objectives of
National Policy on Education (NPE) and to further define their new role in the emerging situation. The Committee is informed that
the Standing Committee has considered proposals/requests for Women’s Studies Centre from various Universities and has evolved
a procedure for considering such requests which, inter alia, includes a visit to the concerned University for on the spot selection of
the Centre.   During 2006-07 an amount of Rs.1.98 crore has been provided so far to 42 Centres. Proposals from 104
universities/colleges have been received for the establishment of WSCs, and shall be considered for assistance during the 11
th Plan
period. The Committee welcomes these developments.   The Committee is, however, a bit disappointed to note that only 42 out of
the 100 proposals have been approved by the Department during 2006-07. The Committee urges the Department to speed up the
approval procedure so that all the 104 proposals pending with it could be decided at the earliest. The Committee also recommends

CHAPTER-I
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE GOVERNMENT
 
 
V      RAJIV GANDHI NATIONAL CRECHE SCHEME FOR THE CHILDREN
        OF WORKING MOTHERS    
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
Para 5.4           The Committee was informed that all these three organizations have experience of implementing crèche
programme across the country for almost three decades and have a nation-wide presence and network for running crèches. 
These organizations are well equipped with field units and staff.  Hence no constraints are being faced for implementation of
the scheme through these organizations. The Committee recommends that to meet the growth in number of creches other
organization/NGOs may also be involved in the implementation of these projects.
 
Action Taken
 
To meet the growing need of creches, the Ministry has prepared an EFC paper to open more creches across the country
during the 11th Five Year Plan. While expanding the scheme, due consideration will be given to the recommendations made by
the Committee by involving other reputed organizations/NGOs also for implementation of the crèche programme.
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
Para 5.8           The Committee notes that there are a large number of working mothers in unorganized sector who are in great
need of creches to look after their children when they go to work.  The safety of the children is utterly neglected and they are
prone to score of anti social elements.  Unfortunately, the crèche scheme is not functioning in those areas which need the
most.  The Committee was informed that for opening creches, applications are pending but the Ministry has no funds available
to open the creches.  The Committee therefore recommends that more allocation should be made under this head to meet the
growing demand for creches.  The Scheme may be revamped and expanded and the Planning Commission should be
approached for more allocation emphasizing the need for creches in view of safety of children of working mothers.
 
Action Taken
 
Efforts are being made to revamp and expand the scheme so as to ensure the safety of  the children of the working
mothers. An EFC Memo has been moved for this purpose.
 
 
VI.       SCHEMES TRANSFERRED FROM THE MINISTRY OF SOCIAL JUSTICE AND EMPOWERMENT
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
Para 6.1             A number of schemes have been transferred from the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment to the Ministry
in 2006.  An assessment about their performance during 2006-07 is given below-
 
HOMES FOR INFANT AND YOUNG CHILDREN FOR PROMOTION OF IN-COUNTRY ADOPTION
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
Para 6.8           The Committee wonders why the All India Evaluation is taking such a long time and still not complete. To get
into the fact of the matter the Committee desires to know the details of the procedure of the evaluation, implementing agencies
and time schedule for the evaluation. The Committee may be apprised about the outcome of the evaluation.
 
Action Taken
 
            The National Institute of Public Cooperation and Child Development recently completed its study on “Evaluation of
the Scheme of Assistance to Homes for Children (Shishu Greh) to Promote In-country Adoption”. The study has been
completed within a period of six months and submitted its report  to the Ministry. The study has come out with a positive note

203 rd report on hrd committe
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/203rdreport.htm[01-07-2016 15:45:48]
about the working of the scheme, it has highlighted on the need of supervision/monitoring of these agencies by the State
Governments and CARA in promoting adoptions in the country.
It has been recommended that for effective and smooth functioning of these organisations, timely release of grants is very
essential, grants to on-going projects may be released directly by CARA, new cases will be brought before the Project
Sectioning Committee for approval.
 
            The report has been prepared after analyzing the selected indicators/ parameters and minimum standards provided by
the Ministry which were considered crucial for evaluation of the scheme. A multi-stage stratified random sampling technique
was applied to select state-wise total number of organisations at the first stage. At the second stage, purposive sapling method
was applied for selection of the organisations. Brief of the outcome of the evaluation study is placed at Annexure-IX.
 
A copy of the report was sent to the Department of Expenditure, Ministry of Finance to consider lifting the ban
imposed on expansion of this scheme. In reply, the Department of Expenditure has communicated that since the Ministry of
Women and Child Development is formulating a new scheme –‘Integrated Child Protection Scheme (ICPS)’ by incorporating
the elements of the schemes i, e, An Integrated Programme for Street Children, Scheme for Assistance to Homes (Shishu
Greh), CARA and Child line, etc, there is no justification for the expansion of scope of the existing scheme which are under
consideration.
.X.       CENTRAL ADOPTION RESOURCE AGENCY (CARA)
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
Para 11.3         Rajiv Gandhi Scheme for Empowerment of Adolescent Girls is another new scheme proposed to be launched
after merger of two schemes, Kishori Shakti Yojana and Nutrition Programme for Adolescent Girls. The Committee observes
that NPAG was implemented on a pilot basis in 2002-03 and 2003-04 by the Planning Commission It continued on a pilot
project basis in 51 identified backward districts in 2006-07 also. Kishori Shakti Yojana has been there under ICDS for a few
years. It was only in 2006-07 that the scheme has been expanded from 2000 ICDS projects to 6118 ICDS projects. Committee
is not aware whether there is going to be a significant modification by bringing these two schemes under a new scheme.  The
Committee would, however, like to emphasise that there is a need for having a comprehensive review of all the Schemes
relating to nutrition for women and children being run not only by the Ministry of Women and Child Development but by
other Ministries like Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Rural Development etc.  The Committee strongly feels that there
should be an umbrella scheme for provision of nutrition to women and children under which different small schemes run by
other Ministries can be brought together.
 
Action Taken
 
 Rajiv Gandhi Scheme for Empowerment of Adolescent Girls  is proposed to be launched on merger of Kishori Shakti
Yojana and Nutrition Programme for Adolescent Girls. A proposal for expansion of NPAG to all districts and its merger with
KSY has been included in the XI Plan proposals of the Ministry.  This is necessary to improve the nutritional status of
adolescent girls and also to empower them socially and economically.
 
 The current efforts for addressing the issues of adolescent girls need to be stepped up substantially in an integrated manner. It
is necessary to expand  NPAG [which at present is being implemented in 51 identified districts only] and merge it with   KSY, 
enrich content and expand coverage of merged scheme to all the districts in the country in the XI Plan.  An integrated approach
taking care of life skills, nutrition, health of adolescents may pave way for a healthy society/ better quality human resources. It
would also lead to reduction in IMR/ MMR.
 
The two schemes are planned to be merged since they exist with more or less similar interventions, for the same group of
target beneficiaries. There are no significant modifications as such, envisaged in the new scheme.            However, the
provision for KSY which was prescribed, in the year 1991, as Rs.1.1 lakh per block per annum, is proposed to be revised upto
Rs.5 lakh per block per annum.  This will enrich the content, strengthen the training component and improve the quality of
services by making the interventions more meaningful.
 
 The  ICDS Scheme is not exclusively a Nutrition Scheme, but aims at holistic development of children below 6 years of age
and pregnant women and lactating mothers, through a package of 6 services viz. supplementary nutrition, growth monitoring,
nutrition and health education, immunization,  referral and pre-school education.  Three of the services i.e.  immunization,
referral services and health check up are provided in convergence with the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare.

Recommendations/Observations
 
Para 2.5           In the light of feedback received about the performance  level during the Tenth Plan period, the Committee
would like to emphasise that every conceivable  measure needs to be taken by the Ministry so that shortfall and deviations
from the prescribed financial norms do not occur during the Eleventh  Plan Period.

Para 2.6           The Committee expresses its serious reservation on the trend of Utilisation of allocated funds during 2006-07.
About 38 per cent of fund utilization during the last quarter of the financial year with 15 per cent to be spent during the last
month, i.e. March  goes against the prescribed norms of only 33 per cent utilization during the last quarter. The Committee

would, therefore, like to emphasise that every conceivable attempt should be made for strict compliance of financial norms.
 
Action Taken
 
Up to December 2006, under the Plan schemes 64.85% funds were utilized and in the last quarter of the financial year 2006-07
the percentage of fund utilization was 32.34%. In the month of March 2007, the expenditure was 15.77%, thus exceeding only
by 0.77% over the limit imposed by the Ministry of Finance.  For expenditure in excess of 15% during March 2007, prior

Recommendations/Observations
 
Para 2.7     The Committee has been voicing its concern about the declining trend in both allocation and utilization of funds for
women welfare schemes. For 2006-07, also, in spite of enhanced allocation of Rs. 130.70 crore, expenditure reported upto 16
th
March, 2007 is only Rs. 91.40 crores. Not only this, the Committee notes that it was only in the last quarter that utilization
picked up as expenditure reported upto 31
st December, 2006 was only Rs. 58.75 crore.
 
Action taken
 
The Ministry has noted the Committee’s observations regarding low expenditure in the year 2006-07 especially upto
31st December, 2006.  As explained earlier, the schemes are being revamped during the XIth Plan and  it is expected that more
proposals would then  come forth.
 
III.
             INTEGRATED CHILD DEVELOPMENT SERVICES SCHEME (ICDS)
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
 Para 3.4          Besides that, States like Andhra Pradesh, Gujarat and West Bengal have exceeded the allocated funds, thereby
indicating that funds from the previous year were also available with them.  Both the situations indicate that some inherent
problem-areas continue to persist under the Scheme.  Either the Central funds are not reaching the implementing agencies in
time or States simply do not have the capacity to utilize the enhanced allocation.  The Committee understands that there
already exists a comprehensive four-level monitoring mechanism for ICDS.  The Committee can only emphasise that there is a
need for strengthening the monitoring mechanism so as to regulate the flow of funds and judicious utilization thereof
 
Action Taken
 
The funds released under ICDS Scheme are for committed liabilities towards salaries of ICDS functionaries,  honoraria
of Anganwadi Workers & Helpers and rents etc. Till the year 2006-07 funds were  released to States/UTs generally in two
instalments.  However, in some cases, additional instalments were released in the later part of the year due to reasons like late
receipt of Statements of Expenditure etc. As a result some unspent balances were there with the States/UTs as on 31.12.2006.
 
In pursuance to the directions of Ministry of Finance, from the current financial year i.e. 2007-08, the release of funds
to the States/UTs would be made in four instalments.  To monitor the expenditure more effectively, the release of instalments
has further been linked to receipt of Statement of Expenditure/Monthly Progress Report of the preceding quarter.  This would
lead to reduction in unspent balances at the end of each quarter.
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
Para 3.13  The Committee is aware that the ICDS was envisioned as a community participative programme and the
components of the scheme do not provide for the creation of infrastructural facilities.  However, in view of the present dismal
status of AWC buildings and also chronic problem of fund constraints being faced by majority of States, it is now time that
providing infrastructural facilities like construction of pucca building and other related aspects form part of the scheme so that
over a period of time all the AWCs must have pucca building to function.  If the Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan can provide 30% of
its allocation for infrastructure development, the Committee does not find any reason why a particular percentage of the fund
could not be allocated for infrastructure creation under the ICDS.
 
Action Taken 
 
Taking cognizance of the fact that there is no provision for construction of AWCs under the  ICDS Scheme, except in

To address this issue, the Government under the proposed revamped ICDS Scheme is contemplating infrastructural
development, on the pattern of SSA/NRHM. It is proposed to earmark 30% of the funds allocated for the ICDS scheme for
infrastructure development, including construction of AWC buildings, baby friendly toilets, provision of safe drinking water
etc.  
Since the number of AWCs without adequate infrastructure is very large, it has also been decided to explore the
possibilities of tapping the funds available under existing Schemes/Programmes of other Ministries also such as the National

(SCSP), Tribal Area Sub Plan (TASP), etc.  These Ministries have already been requested to consider modifying their existing
guidelines to earmark certain percentage of allocation for construction of Anganwadi Centres.
 
Simultaneously, provision of safe drinking water and toilet facility in an Anganwadi Centre is also being attempted
through convergence with Accelerated Rural Water Supply Programme, Total Sanitation Campaign being administered by the
Department of Drinking Water Supply under the Ministry of Rural Development.

Recommendations/Observations
 
Para 5.6           The other area of concern identified by the Committee is the pendency of settlement of accounts. The

Action Taken
 
The  accounts of all State Boards have been settled up to the year 2005-06 except for Andhra Pradesh State Board for
which the accounts could be settled up to 1995-96 only due to certain  problems in the State Board for which every efforts are
being made to settle the accounts as soon as possible.  The accounts of all aided voluntary organizations under crèche scheme
have been settled up to 2005-06. Funds are released after obtaining utilization certificate from the implementing agencies.
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
Para 5.7
         The Committee notes that the monitoring of crèches which is a continuing process has been assigned to
States/Women study centres of the Universities and State Women Development Corporations during the current financial
year.  So far, feedback has been received from monitoring         agencies in respect of 276 crèches being run in the States of
Delhi, Haryana, Jammu & Kashmir, Madhya Pradesh, Manipur, Nagaland, Orissa, Tripura and Uttar Pradesh. The Committee
may be apprised about the feed back on the implementation of the scheme.
 
Action Taken
 
Feed-back on the implementation of the scheme received from independent monitoring agencies indicates normal
running of the creches excepting a few discrepancies like running of the creches for less duration, shortage of accommodation,

Action Taken
 
            As per Section 4 of the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2000, the State Government, by
notification in the Official Gazette, constitutes for a district or a group of districts specified in the notification, one or more
Juvenile Justice Boards for exercising the powers and discharging the duties conferred or imposed on such Boards in relation
to juveniles in conflict with law under this Act. A Board shall consist of a Metropolitan Magistrate or a Judicial Magistrate of
the first class, as the case may be designated as Principal Magistrate and two social workers as Members of the Board.  The
Principal Magistrate and Members of the Board are appointed by the State Governments.
           
            As per Section 14(2) of the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Amendment Act, 2006, the Chief
Judicial Magistrate or the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate shall review the pendency of cases of the Board at every six months,
and shall direct the Board to increase the frequency of its sittings or may cause the constitution of additional Boards.
  
All the State Governments/ UT Administrations have been requesting from time to time take appropriate actions for
proper implementation of the provisions of the Act in true spirit.
    
            The information regarding number of cases pending in Juvenile Justice Board alongwith their period of pendency are
not maintained by the Ministry. However, Ministry is in the process for setting up of detailed database on juvenile system in
the country, information regarding number of cases pending in JJB alongwith their period of pendency is part of that exercise.

After Notification of the Amendment Act, 2006 in the Gazette, all the State Governments/ UT Administrations have
been requested to take necessary action for proper implementation of the provisions of the Act on top priority basis.
 
Ministry is implementing a Centrally Sponsored Scheme –“A Programme for Juvenile Justice” under which grant-in-
aids are released to the State Governments/UT Administrations to meet 50 per cent expenditure requirements for
establishment, upgradation  of homes under the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2000 and maintenance
grants of the  children staying in these homes. 
 
As per the norms of the scheme, State Governments/ UT Administrations are required to meet remaining 50 per cent
expenditure from their State Budget. Some of the State Governments like Arunachal Pradesh, Manipur, etc. expressed their
inability to make arrangements of necessary budget provisions in their State Budget to meet remaining 50 per cent expenditure
under the scheme.
 
The UTs like Lakshdweep and Dadra & Nagar Haveli have intimated the Ministry that they do not have problem of
juveniles and there is no home in these UTs under the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2000. If any case
comes to notice, he/she is kept in Working Women Hostel, Khavaratti (Lakshdweep) and by Dadra & Nagar Haveli in
Navisari and Surat districts in Gujarat.
 
The UT of Chandigarh Administration also informed  the Ministry that they did not require central assistance for
running the existing homes in the UT . They are meeting the expenditure from their  State Budget.
 
The State Governments of Uttaranchal  and Pondicherry were release grants of Rs.35,34,686/- and Rs.31,88,560/-
respectively  under the scheme during the financial year 2006-07.
           
The proposals as received under the scheme  from the State Governments of  Himachal Pradesh and Jharkhand  were
not complete. Both the  State Governments were requested  to furnish requisite information to consider the proposals. No reply
has been received so far from the State Governments. As soon as it is received, grants will be released to these State
Governments.
 
Ministry have been requesting all the State Governments/ UT Administrations  from time to time to submit proposals
under the scheme for release of central share of grants to the State Governments/ UT Administrations but no response has been
received so far from  the State Governments/ UTs like Jammu & Kashmir, Andaman & Nicobar, Daman & Diu, etc.
 
As per Section 8(1) of the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2000, any State Government may
establish and maintain either by itself or under an agreement with voluntary organisations, observation homes in every district
or a group of districts, as may be required for the temporary reception of  any juvenile in conflict with law during the pendency
of any inquiry regarding them under this Act.
 
As per Section 34(1) of the Act, the State Government may establish and maintain either by itself or in association with
the voluntary organisations, children’s home, in every district or group of districts, as the case may be, for the reception of
child in need of care and protection during the pendency of any inquiry and subsequently for their care, treatment, education,
training, development and rehabilitation.
           
There is no restriction on the number of homes to be set up by the State Government for the juveniles under the Act. It
is subject to conditions that (i) homes has been set up/notified by the State Governments in the Official Gazette; and (ii) the
State Government has made necessary budget provision in the State Budget to meet 50 per cent expenditure of these homes.
           
In the last financial year 2006-07, the Government of Maharashtra submitted proposals to the Ministry seeking
financial assistance for 273 homes covering 15,520 beneficiaries. The State Government had made budgetary provision of
Rs.914.26 lakhs in their State Budget to meet  remaining 50 per cent expenditure of these homes under the scheme. The
Ministry examined the proposal keeping in view the norms of the scheme and released Rs.5,97,32,735/- for the financial year
2006-07.

Comments of the Committee
 
The Committee is constrained to observe that there is only marginal improvement in the pendency of Utilization
Certificates as per the updated information submitted to it by the Ministry.  Against 6765 UCs reported last, total number of
pending UCs as on 31
st July, 2007 is 6467.  What is more worrisome is that against the maximum number of 4697 outstanding
UCs pertaining to the earliest period (1986-87 to 2001-02), latest figures are 4679.  The Committee is compelled to conclude
that serious efforts and constant review claimed to have been made by the Ministry have failed to make any impact on the UCs
outstanding for last two decades.  The Committee also apprehends that records for this period may not be available with the
Ministry.  Had they been available, Committee’s direction for furnishing details of implementing agencies (State-wise,

st  April, 2006 to Rs.

pending only when relaxations are obtained from the Ministry of Finance on case-to-case basis, keeping in mind the smooth
functioning of the schemes.  The Committee finds it hard to believe that the Ministry of Finance would have given relaxation
in a routine manner keeping in view such a large number of UCs remaining outstanding for yeas together.

Recommendations/Observations
 
Para 3.10         The Committee strongly recommends that immediate corrective measures need to be initiated on the gap areas
highlighted in the NIPCCD Study.  If this is the state of affairs after more than thirty years of ICDS being launched and crores
of funds being provided under the Flagship Scheme of the Ministry, then it would be better if the so-called multi-level
monitoring mechanism is simply done away with.
 
Action Taken   
 
The Evaluation Study entitled ‘Three Decades of ICDS: An Appraisal’ conducted by NIPCCD in December, 2006 was
circulated to all State Governments/UTs.  A presentation was also made in the Conference of State Secretaries dealing with
ICDS requesting them to take urgent steps to rectify the deficiencies pointed in the Study.
 
It may, however, be noted that ever since its launch in 1975, the Scheme does not provide for construction of AWC
building or safe drinking water/sanitation facilities in the AWCs.  It was envisaged that the local community would provide the
infrastructure.  There has been, though, provision for hiring a suitable building on rent. To enable the Angawandi Workers to
deliver the services under the Scheme efficiently, it has been proposed to provide for construction of AWC building including
kitchen and toilet in the 11th Five Year Plan. Action has been intensified to provide safe drinking water and toilet facilities in
the anganwadi centre through convergence with schemes like Accelerated Rural Water Supply Programme, Total Sanitation
Campaign being administered by the Ministry of Rural Development.  Efforts are also being made, as the requirement of funds
is very large, to explore the possibility of utilizing funds available under existing schemes of various Ministries like NREGA,
Backward Region Grant Fund, MPLADS and SCSP, TASP etc. for strengthening the infrastructure at AWC.
 
The Statements of Expenditure sent by the States have a column specifying procurement of PSE kits.  It is reflected
from the SOEs  that some of the States were not procuring PSE kits as per their entitlement. These States have been requested
to procure the same at the earliest so that the benefit of PSE reaches all the beneficiaries.  There is a provision of Rs. 5000/- in
the Scheme for purchase of cooking and serving utensils among other things at the time of operationalisation of AWCs.  There
is also a provision of contingencies at AWCs level of Rs. 600/- which could be used for replacement of utensils.
 
It has also been observed from the expenditure statement received as on  31.3.07 that many States have spent more than
their allocated share of Supplementary Nutrition. However, (12 out of 23 which reported) States which have not been incurring
90 per cent of their estimated expenditure of the SNP budget were requested to spend as per the norms by providing adequate
funds in their budget of 2007-08 (Assam and Orissa are part of theses 12).
 
The States have also been requested to utilize the available amount of Rs 25,000 per project for IEC activities so that

under active consideration.

scenario.  If the State-wise figures are analysed, shortfall and gaps are noticed across the country. The Committee is extremely 
disturbed to note that there are States where need is the maximum, but out of less than half of targeted children covered under

XI        NEW SCHEMES
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
Para 11.2         Committee’s experience about new schemes proposed to be launched by the Ministry has not been very
encouraging. Committee has been observing that new schemes are proposed without any preliminary exercise about
formulation of their components.  A token provision is duly made which continues for years together due to a number of
procedural formalities to be completed at different levels. New schemes should be announced only after the text of the scheme
is ready.  Comprehensive Scheme for Combating Trafficking of Women and Children and Scheme for Relief and
Rehabilitation of Rape Victims are two such schemes. Comprehensive Scheme for Combating Trafficking of Women and
Children was introduced during the Tenth Plan.  As per the information available with the Committee, there was an allocation
of Rs. 3.00 crore for the Scheme in 2004-05, reduced to Rs. 30 lakhs in 2005-06 and Rs. 50 lakhs provided in 2006-07.
Provision for 2007-08 is Rs. 1.00 crore. The only progress which seems to have been made is the change in its name. The very
fact that it is proposed to be launched as a new scheme inspite of being in the formulation stage during the Tenth Plan indicates
that there is not going to be any progress in the near future.  Scheme for Relief and Rehabilitation  of Rape Victims is the other
scheme which was introduced in 2006-07 with a token provision of Rs. 1.00 crore. Same provision is there for 2007-08 and it
continues to be at the proposal stage.

analyzing with State implementing agencies the problem areas and finding out the ways and means to tackle the same.  The
Committee strongly feels that along with the implementing agencies, time has also come for reaching out to the targeted
beneficiaries directly. Once, they are made aware, through media and local authorities, the multi-level monitoring mechanism
will get the real strength and lead to fulfillment of all the objectives of this Flagship Scheme of the Ministry.                     
                                                                                    (Para 3.10)
 
Comments of the Committee
 
            The Committee notes that attempts of the Ministry for creating a database on the infrastructural facilities available at
AWCs have not proved to be very successful.  Information from only 18 States has been received and the major States like
Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Madhya Pradesh, Jammu & Kashmir, Chattisgarh, West Bengal, Tamil Nadu and Andhra Pradesh are
still to send the information.  The Committee strongly feels that average percentage of pucca building of AWCs would come
down once data from all the States/UTs is available.  The Committee finds that  data from 30 States/UTs is available so far as
availability of drinking water and toilet facilities at AWCs is concerned.  In these 30 States, having 5,55,459 AWCs, 30.8%
AWCs neither have toilet nor drinking water supply, and only 8.68% AWCs having both the facilities.  Here also major States
like Bihar, Assam, Karnataka, Jammu & Kashmir are not included.  Condition of AWCs will make a dismal reading, if data
from all the operational 8,44,743 AWCs is available. The Committee apprehends that ground realities would prove to be more
disheartening as this data is mainly based on the information sent by State Governments.                                 (Para 3.12)
 
Comments of the Committee
 
            The Committee is happy to note that the Ministry is considering revamping of the Scheme and implementing it is a
“Mission Mode on the pattern of Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan and Natilonal/Rural Health Mission” in the 11
th Plan period.  The
Committee however, would like to remind that the 11 th plan period has begun and this exercise should be finalized at the
earliest for the timely implementation of the scheme with its new facets.  Preparatory exercises like setting up of State and
District level societies for ensuring smooth and timely flow of funds and apprising the PRIs, SHGs of women, State-holders
Committee such as Mothers Committee etc of their involvement in motivation and support to the scheme, need to be done
beforehand.  The Committee is of the view that experience of the Ministries of Human Resource Development and Health and
Family Welfare so far in administering SSA and NRHM in Mission Mode may be shared by the Ministry so as to ensure a
fully effective monitoring mechanism under ICDS.                   (Paras 3.14 & 3.16)
 
Comments of the Committee
The Committee observes that there is no noticeable improvement so far as children            (6 months-6 years) receiving
supplementary nutrition is concerned.  Out of 15.78 crore eligible children, 10.49 crore children were covered under ICDS and
only 5.43 crore children were receiving supplementary nutrition as on 30
th September, 2006.  The Committee finds that
position remains unchanged as on 31 st March, 2007.  Out of 10.76 crore children under ICDS, only 5.82 crore children were
getting supplementary nutrition.  It seems that regular review and monitoring of the coverage of beneficiaries has failed to
make any difference as in 13 States, less than 50% child population was being covered.  Coverage in States like Assam
(26.04%), Bihar (35.92%), Kerala (35.40%), Rajasthan (33.03%), Jammu & Kashmir (37.13%) was very discouraging.  The
Committee fails to understand the constraints for supplementary nutrition not being provided to all the children registered in an
AWC when required finds were reported to be available.  Latest data made available to the Committee indicates that in the
case of many States, release of State-share seems to have been delayed as major expenditure is reported to be made during the
last quarter of the year.

            Hence, the Committee recommends that the Ministry should ensure timely release of funds to the States.  Also, close
monitoring and review of the implementation of scheme and coverage of Ministries needs to be carried out on a regular basis
for effective operationalisation of the Scheme.                                                                            (Para 3.18)
 
Comments of the Committee
 
            The Committee would appreciate if feedback about the bottlenecks/problem areas besides paucity of funds, being faced
by the States lagging behind in making supplementary nutrition available to the targeted children, is furnished to it.    (Para
3.19)  
 
Comments of the Committee
 
            While examining the Demands for Grants of the Ministry for 2007-08, the Committee was informed that the Review
Committee to examine the current levels of honorarium and related issues of Anganwadi Workers and Helpers set up on the
22
nd September, 2006, had submitted its Report which was under the consideration of the Government.  Committee in its
Report presented to the Parliament on the 27th April, 2007, had hoped that a final view on the recommendations of the Review
Committee would be taken at the earliest.  The Committee, however, is surprised to note that although more than a year has
passed since the submission of Review Committee Report, it still continues to be under the consideration of the Ministry as no
Status Report has been given in the Action Taken Note.  The Committee takes a serious view of this and impresses upon the
Ministry to do the needful without any further delay.                                                 (Para 3.23)
 
Comments of the Committee
 
Acute shortage of Anganwadi Workers, Helpers and Supervisors, the three key functionaries of an Anganwadi Centre
in all the States, has been engaging the attention of the Committee for quite some time.  Latest feedback received from the
Ministry, however, reveals a discouraging scenario.  The Committee is not inclined to agree with the claim of the Ministry that
there has been improvement in the recruitment of AWWs and Helpers as on 31.03.2007, compared with the position as on
30.09.2006.  The Committee also has its reservation about the 62% in-position strength of Supervisors vis-a-vis sanctioned
strength as on 30.09.2006.  Like last year, glaring disparities between the number of sanctioned posts of all the three key
functionaries of AWC in some of the very crucial States continue to persist as revealed in the latest data made available to the
Committee.  The Committee is constrained to observe that in States like Assam, Bihar, Gujrat, Himachal Pradesh, Jammu &
Kashmir, Jharkhand, Nagaland,  Punjab, West Bengal, even all the posts of AWWs and Helpers sanctioned as on 31.03.2005,
have not been filled up upto 31.03.2007.  It is true that posts have been duly sanctioned in subsequent years, but it is very
disturbing to note that not even a single State has succeeded in recruiting AWWs and Helpers against at the posts sanctioned in
2005-06.   Position with respect to Supervisors is more grim.  With only 26,052 Supervisors to oversee 8,44,743 AWCs, one
can imagine the ground realities at such Centres. 
            The Committee has been informed that instructions have already been issued to States/UTs for reservation of 25% of
vacancies of Supervisors for AWWs and similar percentage in vacancies AWWs for AWHs.  Information from 21 States has
been received that 25 percent posts of Supervisors have been reserved to be filled up from AWWs.  The Committee fails to
understand that inspite of such initiatives, sanctioned posts of all the three categories continue to remain vacant.  The
Committee has no option but to reiterate that thorough revamping of the entire recruitment procedure is required to be
undertaken in active co-ordination with States, specially those having the maximum vacancies.
(Paras 3.24, 3.25 & 3.27)
 
Comments of the Committee
 
            The Committee is happy to note that benefits of Anganwadi Kanyakartri Bima Yojana have started reaching the
Anganwadi Workers and Helpers.  The Committee, however, finds that premium of Rs.80/- per beneficiary payable by the
insured Anganwadi Workrs/Helpers has been waived w.e.f. 1.4.07 for a period of two years.  The Committee fails to
comprehend the waiving of premium only for two years.  The Committee reiterates that this facility should be extended to all
concerned without imposing any condition therein.                                                                                                                    
(Para 3.29)        
 
Comments of the Committee
 
            While deliberating on the Demands for Grants of the Ministry for 2007-08, the Committee was informed that a Central
Monitoring Unit had been set up at the National Institute of Public Cooperation and Child Development (NIPCCD) for
monitoring ICDS through independent professional organization in each State/UT.  All the 44 organizations participating in a
workshop conducted by NIPCCD had unanimously agreed to act as select/state level institutions for monitoring of ICDS.  The

Committee was given to understand that detailed guidelines for monitoring were being finalized.  This was the position in
April, 2007.  Since then, more than seven months have passed but the detailed guidelines are yet to be finalized.  The
Committee is not happy with such state of affairs.  The Committee is not aware by when the guidelines would be finalized. 
Only thereafter the process for formally engaging the selected institutions would start.  The Committee has been emphasizing
again and again that schemes should come out of procedural formalities so as to ensure their benefits reaching out to the
targeted beneficiaries.  The Committee can only reiterate that the new monitoring mechanism envisaged for ICDS should be
activated at the earliest.                                                                                                         (Para  3.31)
 
Comments of the Committee 
 
            The Committee notes that 10.53 lakh AWCs have been sanctioned upto 31
st March, 2007 and the third phase of
expansion of AWCs has already been initiated by the Department.  All these AWCs are expected to be operationalized by
December, 2008, the date indicated by the Supreme Court.  The Committee can only say that it is a very ambitious plan as
ground realities are entirely different.  As per the feedback given by the Ministry, out of 10.52 lakh AWCs sanctioned upto
31st March, 2007, 8.44 lakh AWCs were operational on that date.  The Committee would like to point out that all these
operational AWCs could not be considered operational as a large number of AWCs were not having the required manpower. 
In the absence of key functionaries like AWW/Helper/Supervisor, an AWC cannot be considered functional in the real sense. 
The Committee, therefore, observes that Supreme Court directive can only be carried out through an Action Plan in co-
ordination with State Governments at all the levels.                                        (Para 3.32)
 
IV.
              TRAINING PROGRAMME UNDER ICDS
 
Comments of the Committee
 
            Training programme of ICDS functionaries continues to be an area of concern for the Committee.  The Committee had
observed that during the first three quarters of 2006-07, achievement level for training of different functionaries remained well
below the physical targets.  However, the Committee is surprised to note that the last quarter of 2006-07 could be considered
very successful.  It seems that out of the total number of functionaries trained during the entire year; more than half of them
were imparted training during the last quarter.  Even then, overall average rate of training had remained below 50 percent, with
some of the states showing very unsatisfactory level.  Reasons like targets set on the higher side, recruitment of
AWWs/Helpers getting delayed due to elections, delay in administrative sanctions, court cases etc. cited by the Ministry do not
seem to be very convincing.  The Committee would again emphasize that all out efforts need to be made by all concerned so
that all the functionaries under ICDS get proper and timely training.  One must not forget that only trained manpower can play
an effective role in reaching out to the targeted beneficiaries under ICDS.                            (Para  4.4)
 
V         RAJIV GANDHI NATIONAL CRECHE SCHEME FOR THE CHILDREN OF WORKING MOTHERS
 
Comments of the Committee
 
The Committee is concerned with the concentration of crèches in some States. The Committee is happy to note that the
Ministry has initiated action to expand the coverage under the Rajiv Gandhi National Creche Scheme.  The Committee hopes
that uncovered areas would be brought under this scheme during the 11
th Plan in a time bound manner.
(Para 5.5)
 
XI        NEW SCHEMES
 
Comments of the Committee
 
            The Committee has been voicing its deep concern on the practice of launching/announcing of new schemes and their
remaining in formulation stage.  The Committee finds that approach of the Ministry remains unchanged.  The Committee had
highlighted the status of two new schemes in its earlier report.  The Committee is constrained to observe that those two
schemes, ie Comprehensive Scheme for Combating Trafficking of Women and Children and Scheme for Relief and
Rehabilitation of Rape Victims continue to remain in the formulation stage.  While the first scheme awaits the approval of the
Ministry of Finance before its formal launch, in-principle approval from the Planning Commission is awaited in the case of
second scheme.  The Committee can only hope that Comprehensive Scheme for Combating Trafficking of Women and
Children will perhaps be launched in 2008-09.  However, the same expectation cannot be made in respect of the Scheme for
Relief and Rehabilitation of Rape Victims.  The Committee would once again emphasize that the Ministry needs to take the
initiative in minimizing the time required for launch of a new scheme in the real sense.                                                 (Para
11.2)

Comments of the Committee
 
            Malnutrition continues to afflict both children and young mothers in our country, inspite of this problem being tackled
through schemes administered by a number of Ministries including the Ministry of Women and Child Development.  The
Committee had noted earlier that a National Level Coordination Committee consisting of representatives from all the
concerned Ministries had been constituted in the year 2005.  On a specific enquiry about the number of meetings held by this
Committee since its inception, the Committee has been informed that only one meeting has been held by the Coordination
Committee so far.  As a pre-liminary exercise, joint letters have been written to all the States/UTs by the Secretary (WCD) and
Secretary (Health).  States have been directed to set up Coordination Committees at different levels.  A national level
Monitoring Committee under the chairpersonship of MOS(WCD) was set up in February, 2007.  The Committee does not
anticipate any significant outcome of these initiatives, reason being that different authorities are yet to be set up and if
constituted, yet to meet.  The Committee strongly feels that the Ministry of WCD needs to take a more pro-active role by
having a regular interaction with the local/state authorities of pockets showing high level of malnutrition.  Only then one can
think of ensuring that our children do not continue to suffer from malnutrition.                                                                 
                        (Para 11.4)
 
Comments of the Committee
 
The Committee finds it unfortunate that such an important body like National Nutrition Mission (NNM), which is
headed by no less than Hon'ble Prime Minister has not met even once since its inception in July, 2003.  The Executive
Committee and the said Core Group, it appears have not been as serious as it should have been.  Instead, Ministry has tried to
justify unsuccessfully by citing reasons like national advocacy, sensitization, etc.  The Committee feels that the Ministry
should be more serious on the matter.
(Para 11.5)
 
Comments of the Committee
 
            The Committee is not aware whether comments sought by August 13, 2007 has been received or not & also the
meeting of EFC has taken place or not.  The Committee would like to know the status of the scheme as nearly three quarters of

country at one go and not in phases.                                          (Para 11.6)

Group on Condensed Courses of Education for women submitted in May, 2006, i.e. more than a year ago.  The Committee
fails to understand the reasons for unduly long time being taken by the Ministry in the matter.  Ministry’s response of a
reminder sent to it for expediting the approval of the recommendations made by the Working Group makes little sense.  The
Committee can only hope that the Ministry would take a final view and revamp the Scheme of Condensed Courses for Women
Education as suggested by the Working Group.  The Committee reiterates its earlier recommendation of expediting the
implementation of the revised programme as recommended by the Working Group from the very outset of 11
th Plan period.

BALIKA SAMRIDDHI YOJANA (BSY)

in complex procedural formalities.  Situation becomes more grave if huge amount of public funds are also involved and
unaccounted for.  The Committee would like to remind the Ministry that yet another plan period has started without things

I.          INTRODUCTION

8.2       The Committee notes that the budgetary allocation for Youth Hostels has decreased to Rs.1.25 crore in BE 2007-08

till September, 2006 under Youth Hostel scheme.  The Committee notes with concern the continuously low utilization of
funds under this scheme. Against an allocation of Rs.4.50 crore in 2005-06, the Ministry could utilize only 1.49 crore.
Further in 2006-07, against an allocation of Rs.3.50 crore, the Ministry could spend a mere Rs. 7 lakh only till 31.12.2006.
The extremely low utilization of funds has severely affected the construction of Youth Hostels. The Committee is
perturbed over such a poor performance of an important scheme from its inception. It recommends the Ministry to make
effort to improve the situation and devise specific measures to address various problems associated with this scheme.
 
Action Taken
 
            It may be clarified that during the year 2005-06, an expenditure of Rs.1.05 crores was incurred under the Scheme
upto June, 2005.  The expenditure was Rs.2.45 crores upto September 2005 and Rs.3.84 crore upto December, 2005. 
Thereafter, a total of Rs.4.28 crores was spent upto March, 2006.  Ministry has utilized the funds of Rs.4.28 crores (and
not Rs.1.49 crore) against an allocation of Rs.4.50 crores during 2005-06.  Hence, it would not be correct to say that
utilization of funds were extremely low during 2005-06.  Similarly, during the year 2006-07, against an allocation of

release of approved funds.  These funds are released in suitable instalments to ensure its expeditious utilization which also

Commonwealth Games, SAI through its TEAMS Division must have planned for a glittering success in the event.

10.1     On the promotion of traditional/indigenous games, the Ministry informed the Committee that SAI has undertaken
specific initiatives in this regard and that it has adopted 27 indigenous games and martial arts and about 504 trainees
availing some scholarship/financial assistance have been covered. The Committee notes that there is no specific scheme
for promotion of traditional/indigenous games. Only those games which are falling in the category of Olympic disciplines
are being looked after by SAGs and STC Centers. Also there are few National Sports Federations that look after few
indigenous games that are recognized as an Olympic discipline. The Committee strongly feels that traditional/indigenous
games have not been given due attention as there appears to be no scheme specifically for this purpose. The Committee is
of the opinion that the traditional/indigenous games need not only be preserved but be also promoted in a planned manner.
The Committee disapproved this piecemeal approach in this regard. The Committee, therefore, emphasizes the need for a
focused policy to promote traditional indigenous games. It is of the opinion that Ministry should take all necessary steps
urgently with a clear vision to achieve the goal.

scouting of talent in these games for nurturing in modern sports, the Governing Body of SAI in its 28

2.5.11  The Committee during its on-the-spot-visits found that upkeep and basic infrastructure/amenities in the primary
schools needed special attention. Similarly, participation of village education/ school management Committees was
conspicuous by its absence. It needed to be strengthened in a big way as it is the prime mover of the SSA. Toilets in this
region were virtually non-existent in many schools visited by the Committee. Wherever toilets were, they were common
and in a very bad shape. These components need special and urgent-attention by the State Government.
 
Action Taken
 
Upto 2005-06, 4448 toilets have been provided under SSA to J&K. Also State has been advised to converge with the Total
Sanitation Programme and the Drinking Water Mission to provide drinking water & toilet facilities in schools.
 
Recommendation/Observations
 
2.5.12  The Committee notes the progress of SSA in J&K with satisfaction as regards allocating State’s share, increasing
enrolment as well as reducing out-of-the school children gradually. However, the State did not seem to have district-wise
data regarding dropouts from the schools. The Committee feels that districts like Poonch, Rajauri, Doda, Kargil and
Budgam need special  attention which have higher ratio of out-of-school children. Focused attention is required for
education of ST girls belonging to Bakerwal, Gujar and Gaddi tribes. The problem of child labour in carpet weaving and
paper making industry in some districts (e.g. Budgam) also needs greater attention.

State has decreased its OoSC from 377170 (2002-03) to 108560 (2006). Funds for various flexible strategies are being

KGBVs after bridging.

2.5.14  There appears to be a huge backlog in training teachers, an important component of SSA. The Committee
recommends that a detailed strategy should be chalked out for training the teachers in a time-bound manner and

Action Taken
 
In J & K, teacher training needs are identified at the cluster level and are communicated to, collated and prioritized at
Zonal, District and State levels. State level as well as District level teacher training institutes (SIEs, DIETs) conduct
studies and reviews regarding teacher competence and area specific training needs. Based on zone specific and district
specific need assessment, ZRCs and DRGs have the freedom to adapt the training programmes to suit local needs and
circumstances.  
 
During 2006–07, the training was conducted exclusively in a trainee-active mode with least scope for lectures. Training
methods pursued included:
•         Group discussion & group work
•         Individual assignments
•         Presentation of good practices
•         Development of TLM
MHRD and Pedagogy Unit (TSG), in collaboration with Rajiv Gandhi Foundation in 2006 – 07 carried out series of
workshops for overall quality improvement in the State.
Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan (SSA) recognizes the critical role of teachers and to focus on their development needs, a number
of Block Resource Centres and Cluster Resource Centres have been set up. In-service training of teachers of 20-day
duration is organized each year. During 2006-07, a total of more than 23.57 lakh teachers were imparted 20-day training
upto 31.12.2006. In addition, over 1.39 lakh teachers were given Induction Training upto December 2006. Also, over 1.21
lakh untrained teachers were trained upto December 2006.  The content of in-service teacher training is decided by States,
and includes training in teaching English, as per needs.  NCERT is supporting States in reviewing their curriculum and
syllabi in the light of the National Curriculum Framework (NCF), 2005.

2.5.19  The Committee is fully aware of the ground situations prevailing in the State of J&K.  Education can be an

Action Taken
 
The framework for implementation of SSA is not an area specific document but is applicable throughout India. However,
it enjoys enough flexibility for local specific interventions. For e.g., the Annual Work Plan & Budget for SSA, are drawn
up by each district, so as to reflect local needs & priorities.  Though there has to be a conformity to the broad framework
of SSA, yet in norms for civil works, girls education, alternative education centres/ interventions, needs of children with
special needs, training of teachers etc. to name a few, local factors in funding norms are taken into regard.  There is also an
untied innovation fund amounting to Rs. 50 Lakh per district for meeting local specific needs.  The representatives of LEH
& Kargil Development Councils are represented in the Executive Committee & General Council of the State SSA
programme, which are empowered to notify norms relevant to different regions of the State.  Therefore, it is this
relationship which needs to be active so as to contextualize SSA for Leh & Kargil.
 
GOIs efforts are always to release State Government funds on time, but if States fail to clear their Utilization Certificates
which are due or fail to meet their State Share in a timely manner, then it becomes a cause for delay in releasing the next
instalment of Central Share.
 
Recommendation/Observations

participation was the bedrock of this mission-mode programme. They may also be involved in formulating educational
curriculum specific to the different areas within the Leh and Ladakh regions. The Leh and Ladakh conditions must be kept
uppermost while laying own guidelines of SSA and other such schemes. The Government of India must bring out
necessary changes in the guidelines of Central/Centrally Sponsored Schemes to suit the conditions of these regions.

V.        IMPLEMENTATION OF SSA IN NORTH EASTERN STATES
 
Recommendation/Observations
 
5.1       The Committee discussed this issue with State Government officials from the North Eastern States and visited
schools in Assam, Manipur and Arunachal Pradesh.  The Committee found that all the States in the North East had begun
the SSA after some initial reluctance.  The expenditure figures showed very encouraging trend in this regard.  For example
while Assam spent 90 per cent of funds allocated in 2004-05, Nagaland spent 90.5 per cent, Mizoram 94 per cent and
Tripura spent as high as 99.8 per cent of the allocation.  Utilization of funds by Sikkim was 63 per cent, Meghalaya 60 per
cent, Manipur 65 per cent and Arunachal Pradesh around 55 per cent.  Main problem faced by NE States the Committee
found, was in providing their share.  All of them have severe financial constraints of their own.  The Committee was
informed that recently it was decided not to revise the sharing pattern of 75:25 as such, between the Center and the States. 
To tide over the financial difficulties of the North Eastern States, however 15 per cent of their share, as a special case, was
decided to be made available from the non-lapsable funds of the Ministry of Development of North Eastern Region
(DONER).  As a result, effectively, this share has since become 90:10 between Centre and NE States.
 
Action Taken
 
Noted.
 
Recommendation/Observations
 
5.2       The Committee welcomes this decision of the Central Government and hopes that the NE States would utilize this
opportunity to implement the programme with renewed vigour.  Regarding future requirements of funds, the States should
mobilize their own resources to fund the State share.
 
Action Taken
 
Noted.

(ii)        The Ministry engaged an independent agency, i.e. Institute of Public Auditor of India to provide a concurrent

VII.     OBSERVATIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
 
Recommendation/Observations
 
7.1       The Committee notes that the problems of North Eastern States are peculiar which are different from those in rest
of the country. Apart from low level of economic development, these States including J&K are faced with large scale law
and order problems including militancy. Most of the States are not in a position to release their share due to their limited
revenue base. The pace of construction of school buildings and additional class-rooms, toilets etc. is quite slow. The per
unit construction cost is very high due to the difficult terrains, harsh climate and inaccessibility of human habitations.
Transportation of goods & materials to schools makes every thing highly expensive. In fact even within the sanctioned
project area, the programme does not reach every settlement. Many of these States are using funds under PMGY
(Pradhan Mantri Gramodaya Yojana) to substitute rather than supplement the funds allocated.
 
Action Taken
 
It is fact that the pace of construction of civil works activities in comparatively slower due to transportation bottleneck,
harsh climate, law and order problems including insurgency. The per unit construction cost is governed under influence of
above stated factors.
 
Recommendation/Observations
 
7.2       Most of the States have, therefore, demanded that the funding pattern for NE States may be revised to 90:10
between the Centre and the States. The Committee feels that their demands needs serious consideration, particularly in
view of the small internal revenue base of the North Eastern States & J&K. The Committee also recommends that the per
unit cost of civil works may be revised keeping in view the difficult terrain/geographical conditions of these States. The
Committee wishes to point out that the problem of increasing amount of State-share every year is due to increase in annual

205th COMMITTEE ON HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT

allocation for SSA every year. Some NE States, therefore, demanded that it should be made hundred per cent centrally
funded scheme. In view of this, the Committee also feels that feasibility of this proposal deserves serious consideration.
 
Action Taken
 
The Central Government has now prescribed a funding pattern of 90:10 for implementation of SSA programme in North
Eastern States during XIth Plan.
The Govt. of India is not determining the unit cost of construction of school building, additional classroom, drinking water
and toilets etc. The unit cost of these items is based on Basic Schedule Rates (BSR) of State Public Works Deptt. The State
Govt. is allowed to determine unit cost on the basis of BSR. Therefore, it is unlikely that construction cost of SSA is high
in comparison to works carry out by Works Deptt. of State”.
 
Recommendation/Observations
 
7.4       The Committee notes with concern that, of the total out-of-school children in the country, 10 per cent are from the
NE States. Another aspect of concern in the North Eastern States is the high drop-out rate; it is as high as 71 per cent in
some States. The Gross Enrolment Ratio, however, is fairly good in this region. Similarly, the pupil teacher ratio in the
North East is also better than the national average. Against a national desirable ratio of 1:40, Arunachal Pradesh has a
ratio of 1:27, Assam has 1:22, Mizoram 1:19, Nagaland 1:12, Sikkim 1:12 and Tripura has 1:23. Yet another area of
concern is the appointment of teachers. The North Eastern States have so far appointed only 5204 teachers, which is
roughly about 34 per cent of the total sanctioned; 66% are yet to be appointed. Besides, the North Eastern States have a
very large number of untrained teachers. The Committee was further informed that the assistance of IGNOU is being
taken for training the teachers through distance education mode.
